Finally, we apply this framework to address the problem of aggregating vectors in federated learning, deriving formulas for over-transmission and transmission complexity, and utilizing this framework to design low-overtransmission codes based on special classes of linear codes.

We establish the Scott domain model of Scott's lambda-calculus with convergence testing within univalent type theory. By redefining the Scott model in terms of continuous functions on Scott domains, we contribute to an existing proof of their universal property in univalent type theory.

This paper focuses on applying Fejer-Lenart Fej\'{e}r-Lenart shift operators to study Eisenstein contributions at the lowest pole of the symmetric square of the spherical Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand series for $GL(n)$. The results extend previous work by Gourevich on elementary particles to a broader context and offer a fejerization expression for the square of the spherical Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand series. The approach draws its methodology from the fejerization work of Fejer-Lenart and supplementary research by Fejer, Mezzadoni, and the second author.

This research explores the development of a safety-focused control method for robotic arms that accounts for their varied configurations. The proposed algorithm utilizes control barrier functions to guarantee collision avoidance and incorporates a model predictive control scheme that in real-time selects the optimal safety parameters based on the robot's configuration, enabling adaptation to dynamic environments and mobile robotic arms with multiple degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we extend this control strategy to address environmental uncertainties through the integration of hyperbox-type set-membership control. Simulation outcomes validate the efficacy and versatility of the proposed control approach.

Text summarisation using the extractive method involves choosing specific sentences to create a concise summary. This study proposes an innovative graph-based approach to facilitate this process. The proposed method applies a sequential sentence analysis to determine the relationship between sentences, effectively labelling them as part of a 'yes-no' classification task. Following this, an algorithm is used to select a path along the graph that maximises the overall classification accuracy. Ultimately, the nodes along this path constitute the proposed summary. When evaluated against other methods on data from the SQuAD dataset, the proposed technique outperformed comparable extractive models in both average F1 score and factual exact match score metrics.

Researchers have suggested that quantum gravity might necessitate the use of nonlinear operators that comply with Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. In an attempt to explore the implications of nonlinearity for quantum theory, we investigate how non-linear operators affect the boson condensate state. We find that certain types of non-linear operations can generate complex, interacting multicondensates with patterns similar to those seen in quantum gravity theories involving non-gravitational bosonic states. However, we find that non-conserved currents associated with phase symmetries in these theories fail to form a closed algebraic structure.

This paper presents two new T-problems involving meromorphic mappings. Specifically, we prove two distinctness theorems for complete Kähler manifolds with negative or trivial Chern class projects onto, a complex projective space, and also a compact Kähler manifold. Our research contributes to the understanding of the distinctness problems and complements existing work in the field.

Polynomial systems with no degenerate points have a well-defined underlying geometric structure. To identify the nondegenerate solution locus of such systems, a new algorithm is proposed that leverages the Euclidean distance matrix of points on a given variety. This approach leverages the fact that the squared distances between points can be represented by linear polynomials in a higher-dimensional space, enabling the computation of a signature for the system based on its degenerate point components. The outcomes of these signatures provide insights into the composition of the system's decomposition into components of varying degrees. Based on these findings, a practical algorithm is developed to isolate nondegenerate components of polynomial systems that satisfy specific algebraic constraints. This method employs strategies including elimination, variable reduction, and the use of Gröbner bases to systematically remove known degenerate components from the system's solution set. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments with polynomial systems from both theoretical and applied fields.

We have measured photon yields at very low momentum ranges for Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV per nucleon pair, finding that photon yield exceeds the expected values from nucleon-nucleon interactions. The ratio of real to prompt meson yields is higher than the average for all momenta, indicating an increase over time. The photons appear to come from the center of the collision and their production rate increases with energy. This phenomenon can be partly attributed to the breakdown of perturbative QCD at high densities and may also be caused by radiative energy loss of partons as they escape the collision zone, based on the parameter $I\beta/E$.

The concept of the Tur\'an norm was first proposed over 30 years ago and it aims to generalize the well-known Tur\'an problem to the scenario where the density of an edge is variable. The particular version of this problem being considered here focuses on complete $k$-partite graphs that have the maximum possible number of edges, specifically those that have the maximum possible chromatic number and are also $\ell_2$-optimal with respect to a given number of vertices, $n$. This note will discuss the minimum possible value of the $\ell_2$-norm of the edge density of such graphs, where the edge density values can only take on the value 0 or 1.

Achieving a smooth, high-resolution visual experience for users is essential when rendering maps, especially when maintaining a low number of pixels. To address this challenge, a novel effective method for eliminating aliasing in line joins of vector maps is proposed, focusing on optimizing pixel consumption for anti-aliasing rendering. By identifying and limiting the areas prone to aliasing based on geometric line characteristics, the method minimizes computational load and avoids rendering non-adjacent pixels. Consequently, the method enables high-performance, anti-aliasing rendering for maps at any resolution while reducing computation. We further propose an implementation of this method within a line rendering engine and demonstrate its feasibility through a series of experiments, showing the method's practical applicability and superiority to existing solutions.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate complex functions. In this study, we explore the benefits of the recently developed transcendental RBF $\phi_c(\cdot)$ over the traditional Gaussian RBF in terms of numerical stability and derive its properties. Utilizing this novel RBF, we develop a new shape preserving quasi-interpolation scheme, which yields superior results compared to those obtained from the standard Gaussian RBF-based method.

The widespread presence of pulsar emissions across the galaxy suggests the existence of numerous pulsars within the pulsating population, extending beyond the well-studied nearby population of 25, with potential influence on the interstellar medium. Given the detection limit of the INTEGRAL satellite, it's estimated that the background emissions from distant pulsars could be 5-10 times greater than those from the nearby population, with some potential impact on the study of the cosmic X-ray background. Although some of these pulsars may be overwhelmed by gas clouds, others could be distinguishable due to their characteristic pulse patterns, allowing the possibility of identifying hundreds or even thousands of distant pulsars through the analysis of their pulse profiles.

The primary goal of weather classification is to determine the prevailing weather condition outdoors. With the expansion of autonomous systems and the internet of weather devices, there is an escalating requirement for accurate weather classification data and networks. Unfortunately, the performance of existing solutions is hindered by the absence of a standardized benchmark dataset, which prevents direct comparison of various approaches. In an effort to tackle this issue, we present a comprehensive dataset, labeled 'WeatherNet', consisting of 10,183 carefully annotated images across five distinct weather categories. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient data augmentation method to enhance the accuracy of existing networks and mitigate overfitting problems. Our research includes an in-depth evaluation of multiple deep neural networks, including 14 open-source models from the TensorFlow Model Garden, using the WeatherNet dataset. The results of this evaluation reveal that our proposed data augmentation method achieves impressive accuracy rates of 90%, 94%, and 96% with the LeNet, ResNet, and VGG models, respectively. The research materials, including the WeatherNet dataset and code, are freely accessible at https://github.com/jeetkumar1/WeatherImages.

This research paper explores the effects of climate change on social norms through three lenses: scientific data on climate change, economic analysis of influence on these norms, and institutional promotion of awareness. By examining scientific findings regarding climate change across three sections, the study highlights science's role in shaping social norms. Focusing on CO2 emissions from climate change and their impact on various countries, the study examines the influence of science on social norms. The analysis delves into scientists' contribution in shaping public perception of climate change. By emphasizing the potential consequences of climate change, the study emphasizes the role of science in influencing social norms. The study also investigates the influence of institutions on social norms regarding climate change. By emphasizing the potential consequences of climate change, the study explores the role of science in influencing social norms. The study's results show that scientists' efforts to raise awareness of climate change have had a significant impact on its social acceptance. Moreover, the study's findings indicate that scientists' efforts to raise awareness of climate change have had a significant impact on its social acceptance.

This report introduces a real-time online model for soft multi-fingered grippers that can adapt to various online control strategies using the online simulation environment Gymsim. The initial section presents gymsim, a programmable 3D deformable object simulation environment supporting both offline and online interactions via an API. The gymsim online model accurately simulates soft grippers' behavior in real-time, enabling the testing of multiple control strategies on actual soft grippers. Furthermore, the report develops a control method based on reinforcement learning utilizing the online simulator, which successfully demonstrates its effectiveness in tasks like object centering, end-effector positioning, and force regulation.

Our objective is to adapt the Organic Evolutionary Algorithm to the domain of Machine Learning, specifically by integrating Generalization as a novel gradient descent method. This approach replaces the traditional gradient descent fully connected layers in Organic ML, aiming to optimize performance on specific datasets, such as the MNIST data set for generalization tests. In this study, we outline the fundamental principles of OEA and generalize its core components to the context of Machine Learning, along with providing a theoretical basis for our approach.

High-energy emissions from powerful galaxies, produced by the activity of supermassive black holes, can serve as important tools for studying the history of galaxy growth.  Research into the development of these black holes during a specific period of cosmic time, around 12 to 13 billion years ago (redshift $z$ of 2.5-3.5), has been well-established thanks to discoveries made by the Chandra X-ray Observatory.  However, there is less understanding of the same process at redshift $z$ greater than 4.5. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's spectroscopic observations, a highly distant galaxy, J2102+6015, has been found. This bright galaxy emits significant amounts of light across the electromagnetic spectrum and allows for accurate measurement of its properties, including a black hole mass of 3.46 million times that of the sun and a black hole accretion rate of 105 times the rate used for typical black holes on Earth. What is more, recent observations of J2102+6015 have revealed that it emits large amounts of X-ray radiation. This discovery is particularly exciting because it suggests that J2102+6015 might be the youngest high-energy galaxy found so far with a mass more than a thousand times the mass used for typical black holes on Earth and is actually forming black-hole radiation instead of just radiation

Lung cancer is a highly fatal disease, and predicting the outcome of treatment is a significant challenge in medicine. In recent years, the advancement of deep learning for the analysis of medical images has provided new insights into patient survival prediction. However, the full potential of this prediction method can only be reached by combining the information from different medical image types and clinical factors. The study's goal is to enhance lung cancer patient survival prediction using a comprehensive dataset of patients and various image types in combination with clinical information. The research employs the development of separate models for each data type and combines the output using a weighted averaging system. The results show a significant improvement in the accuracy of the predicting model compared to the use of individual data types.

In numerous real-life scenarios, individuals struggle to interact with automated systems. For example, they might find it challenging to convey their desired room temperature. To bridge this gap, we employ natural language processing to extract this information and automate task assignments. To do so, we employ natural language understanding models paired with logical inference, effectively simulating human-like state descriptions. This approach is refined by using reinforcement learning to fine-tune the underlying neural networks.

A novel approach based on machine learning has been developed to derive quasar density powers from absorption feature powers in quasar spectra, addressing a longstanding challenge in astronomy. Traditional models struggled with this task due to the intricate quasar spectrum composition and the limited understanding of early universe matter distribution. Our research demonstrates that machine learning can accurately predict quasar density powers from absorption features, leveraging the intricate patterns within spectra. This breakthrough enables precise power measurements, ultimately leading to a reliable estimation of quasar density bias across various redshifts and spatial scales. Our findings also indicate that machine learning can accurately reconstruct the quasar best-fitting models. This groundbreaking technique marks a significant advancement in quasar research, unlocking new avenues for investigation into the early universe's matter distribution characteristics.

This research explores certain modules over the Lie algebras of differential operators on the real line, specifically those whose restrictions to the zero module are irreducible. We establish that modules with irreducible restrictions are both homogeneous and cyclic. Furthermore, we delve into a specific subcase and develop complete classifications for both the cyclic and homogeneous cases.

The rapidly evolving social media landscape demands the capability to extract valuable insights from user-generated content on platforms like Twitter. With over 260 million active monthly users generating billions of tweets, analyzing sentiment towards specific subjects becomes essential for businesses and organizations. To meet this need, we propose an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework for automatically sentiment analyzing tweets. Our approach is capable of handling varied content lengths, making it applicable to a wide range of texts. Our model achieved accurate results on two publicly available datasets, reflecting its effectiveness in the diverse Twitter environment.

Recent breakthroughs with open-domain dialogue systems have drawn substantial research interest, exemplified by the WSDM 2022 LAMALDIA challenge. While the employed LAMALDIA models are effective, their lack of adherence to specified roles results in unprofessional responses, particularly for character-based systems. To overcome this limitation, this work presents a new approach, featuring a system based on a large-scale language model that ensures role-compliant dialogue. By integrating prompt design and chain-of-thought strategies, our model excels at generating responses aligned with distinct character personalities or tones. Experimental findings indicate superior performance compared to LAMALDIA's best entry, with role compliance significantly enhanced and system coherence and fluency also improved.

New sources of gravitational wave backgrounds are being studied, and one of them arises from the memory effect in gravitational waves. Memetastic gravitational waves are highly nonlinear and cannot be compared to the typical effects of binary mergers, as they thrive in the presence of continuous gravitational wave sources. In areas with continuous sources, memetastic waves are produced at twice the frequency and the characteristic amplitude of the underlying signal. It has been determined that the memory effect contributes significantly to the gravitational wave background in the frequency range of 0.1-10 Hz. When considering the gravitational wave background formed by both the memory effect and the binary merger process, it is possible to detect it using memetastic waves even in scenarios where the background formed by binary mergements is less significant. The sensitivity of current and upcoming detectors, such as LIGO, VIRGO and the space-based detector LISA, could potentially pick up these waves.

A scientifically plausible phase transition of cosmic significance could create gravitational waves and black holes in measurable amounts.  This is particularly true if the phase transition arises from a SUSY-breaking potential with multiple minima.  The structure of this potential depends on a set of complex parameters, which could facilitate a strong first-order phase transition at around 10 TeV.  This  outcome  could generate gravitational waves with the right strength to be detected by upcoming space-based observatories and also lead to the formation of black holes within the required range to create micro-black holes at the LHC. Furthermore, this mechanism could also be the source of baryon asymmetry through out-of-equilibrium decays within the bubbles of this phase transition, occurring at energies where the masses of the right-handed neutrinos are also around 10 TeV. This research investigates various models of such a phase transition at energies where right-handed neutrinos are as heavy as 10 TeV. This  outcome  could lead to a range of outcomes ranging from the production of black holes as small as those detectable at the LHC up to the generation of a detectable signal of gravitational waves in the range of detectability of the LIGO. This  outcome  could also serve as the source of baryon asymmetry at energies where the masses of the right-handed neutrinos are also around 10 TeV. This research demonstrates that the LHC could potentially detect the same phase transition that generated both the gravitational waves

Recent breakthroughs in AI, such as the development of large language models and neural machine translation, have made significant progress in the field of NMT. However, the pervasive issues of ambiguity and data manipulation in real-world communications are not adequately addressed by these advancements. To effectively handle complex interactions, a model must incorporate causal understanding and semantic understanding, ultimately requiring a level of cooperative behavior akin to that seen in signaling games. This study presents an innovative approach that merges neuro-symbolic causal representation learning with the dynamics of signaling games to achieve a cooperative semantic understanding of complex representations, such as Landmark Single Shot Detectors. The results of our simulations and evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the substantial benefits of this novel model.

The Ordinal Term Frequency technique is a widely recognized method for estimating sparse terms in word count matrices, yet it struggles to accurately predict novel terms outside of a model's training data. Our approach combines Ordinal Term Frequency with information hidden in the data matrix to boost word count predictions. When compared to established methods on various datasets, our hybrid model performs on par with Ordinal Term Frequency in counting existing words. However, it surpasses Ordinal Term Frequency in accurately predicting new words.

User preferences can shift quickly, especially in the context of session-based recommendations where a user's interests may change from one visit to the next. Researchers are increasingly focusing on these fleeting user preferences, but existing approaches are often hindered by the need to retrain models every time the data changes, making them impractical for real-world applications. Inspired by the concept of rank-embeddings used in knowledge management, where dynamic user queries can be effectively addressed, we propose a new system that embeds the order in which candidate items are recommended, allowing the model to adapt to changing user preferences without constant retraining. Our strategy involves a two-stage recommendation process, starting with a broad exploration and followed by refining the choice based on real-time feedback. We also devised efficient techniques to accelerate the choice refinement and accelerated the overall recommendation process by choosing to focus on critical probabilities. Through comprehensive testing on both public and practical datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our session-based recommendation strategy and surpass the state-of-the-art models under diverse evaluation criteria.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in arranging and organizing particles that spontaneously organize without any obvious external influence. The formation of clusters from these self-organizing units, known as colloidal molecules, has potential applications across different fields. However, the behavior and properties of these units at the interface with larger molecules have not been fully understood. A new study presents a model where the first type of particles are stabilized by multiple external factors and the second type of particles are attracted to areas with higher concentrations of the first type. The interaction between these two types of particles results in the formation of colloidal molecules and clusters. The study finds that the presence of particles that are attracted to the first type can result in the formation of stable, moving and oriented molecules consisting of the second type of particles. The presence of particles that are attracted to areas with higher concentrations of the first type also has an effect on the phase behavior of the system, which can be understood by considering the interactions between the different types of particles. The study's findings have significant implications for the design and production of materials, which can be further improved by incorporating the present model into the existing tools and techniques used for the design and manufacturing of different materials.

Our research encompasses several innovative approaches to modeling discrete fracture networks. Firstly, we developed an original 3D discrete fracture matrix (DFM) framework based on throughflow and full displacement models. This involves the development of a novel 3D DFM mesh generation technique that ensures seamless integration and accurate representation of fractures within the model. Secondly, we implemented a newly developed Mimetic Finite Difference (MFD) method to solve for Discrete Fracture Matrix model solutions. By leveraging industry standard techniques, we ensured consistency and robustness of our 3D DFM models. Through these advancements, we successfully produced and visualized several test cases, which we then utilized to demonstrate the capabilities and benefits of our technique over other available methods in the literature.

This study introduces an innovative approach where a team of drones cooperates to fly in formation, maintaining a structured pattern in 3D space. Each drone in the formation functions as a collaborative agent, adjusting its position to keep the formation intact. The implementation utilizes a decentralized method where each drone only interacts with nearby peers over a local network. A key feature of this approach involves utilizing a genetic algorithm to optimize formation flight paths and avoid obstacles in the environment's geometry.

In graph theory, the Seidel matrix of a graph G is defined based on its adjacency matrix, where its entries represent the friendship status of vertices in G. The Seidel spectrum of G refers to the eigenvalues of its Seidel matrix. Recent research has established a relationship between the Seidel spectrum and the range and spectrum of a graph G's adjacency matrix. The maximum possible range and minimum energy of the Seidel spectrum for a (0,1)-free graph on n vertices is being investigated, with a focus on proving these extremes for chain graphs and providing a condition for achieving them.

We propose a novel mean-field optimal control problem for stochastic differential equations with fractional Brownian motion delays. To address this problem, we first establish a corresponding mean-field mean-variational dual problem. By utilizing the first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field mean-variational dual problem, we derive the first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field optimal control problem. Furthermore, under specific convexity assumptions, we prove that this first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field optimal control problem is compatible with the first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field mean-variational dual problem, thereby confirming that the first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field optimal control problem are indeed first-order necessary conditions for the mean-field mean-variational dual problem.

The properties of a Dirac operator with non-real spectra are examined, where the spectra are a union of two elliptic finite bands of real values. The research focuses on a scenario with constant magnetization, and spectra that are symmetric around zero. The analysis reveals a zero-index for the operator's associated elliptic self-adjointization under these conditions. Additionally, under a quasi-periodic scenario, the operator's zero-index persists provided the quasi-period is an element of a specific, countable subset of real numbers. However, if the quasi-period is not an element of this subset, the operator exhibits a non-trivial, real-valued, and non-zero topological invariant, known as the Chern number. This invariant can take the values of $\pm 2$. The inherent Dirac magnetic ellipses show a Z_2 symmetry for all magnetization types and demonstrate a duality relationship based on the elliptic T-dual of their generalized K-dual. Furthermore, the ellipses' shapes and types demonstrate a correspondence to local and global topological invariants of the Dirac operator's spectra.

As the demand for wireless connectivity within roadside units increases significantly, it becomes evident that deploying them alone may not be enough to satisfy the rising requirements, especially under high traffic conditions. To mitigate this issue, this research considers the possibility of enhancing a two-layer RSU network by incorporating vehicle relays. The authors establish a mathematical model for the proposed network and analyze key parameters such as vehicle distribution along the highway and vehicle clustering near traffic lights. Furthermore, the study derives the probability of finding a suitable relay vehicle within the specified range and creates models for the formation of vehicle clusters and overall vehicle distribution. The concepts of network area, boundary, and lifetime are introduced to represent the dynamic nature of vehicular networks, which the authors analyze in the context of an Italian traffic system. The research ultimately presents two vehicle relaying protocols, an adaptive and a simplified approach, and evaluates their efficacy in terms of connectivity probability and network throughput.

The goal of the automatically induced label problem is to supplement human expertise with machine decisions on data labeling for tasks like classification. In this study, we explore the possibility of utilizing the dynamic and collaborative platform of Wikipedia to automatically tag articles indicating minor or low-grade edits in the human editing process. We developed three distinct models - one rule-based and two machine learning models - relying on the edited signal to achieve this goal. In contrast to prior work, which was limited to technical domains and relied on static datasets, we successfully applied these models to the entire Wikipedia corpus comprising 5.3 million articles and automatically labeled nearly two million using a labeling signal not manually created. Our empirical evidence shows that the model's predictions align with the actual outcomes of the editing process, specifically in identifying articles prone to minor errors and demonstrating significant model performance advantages over random outcomes. Furthermore, we discovered that articles prone to minor errors are characterized by specific properties such as being shorter in length and associated with fields like medicine.

Deep learning models, specifically binary classifiers, have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of applications. However, their black-box nature limits our understanding of their internal workings. Recent attempts to decipher this mystery through reverse engineering have encountered obstacles. Researchers have found that such models can be effectively deceived by minimally altered input images, known as adversarial examples. In this context, we examine a scenario where an adversary seeks to transfer knowledge from a hidden binary classifier to a new, previously unseen model without access to its source code. By investigating various attacks, including those that utilize minimal changes and targeted transformations, we demonstrate the potential for data and code-free knowledge transfer. Our results reveal the existence of transferred adversarial examples, which are distinct from the original inputs and can successfully evade the now-hidden classifier on new, unseen images. This phenomenon highlights the critical implications of black-box models in a world where they can be easily replicated and disseminated.

We have gathered the largest collections of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays in the context of LHCb's 2016 data analysis. The results show that we have processed $1.7 \times 10^{11}$ $b$-hadron decays, leading to the demonstration of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay with a significant signal of 10.4 standard deviations and a calculated yield of 12.1 decays. The results also include the determination of branching fractions for both $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays, revealing a measured ratio of 0.141 percent for the former and a fraction of 0.090 with regard to the latter. The reported figures account for the uncertainties associated with the measurements.

The cylinder is a fundamental space whose variation is limited to its twisting. When the cylinder is twisted over a manifold with Lorentzian topology, the resulting model's possible T-dual models exceed its potential metric dual models due to the separate transformability of the t-duality and the Holonomy. A new model can be created by exchanging the base and fiber of the original cylinder while also exchanging the t-dual fiber with the base of the model. This exchange results in a duality swap between the base and fiber components of the cylinder.

Reinforcement learning can be enhanced by incorporating imitation learning, which seeks to replicate the expert's ideal behavior. This is achieved by collecting a set of demonstrations from the expert. Nonetheless, obtaining numerous high-quality demonstrations is often impractical or even impossible in many scenarios. Thus, training with only a limited number of demonstrations is essential. We propose a solution by leveraging co-imitation, a technique that enables agents to learn each other's behaviors without direct expert involvement, thereby allowing them to self-generate data. Building upon this concept, we introduce CoRL, a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that utilizes co-imitation for efficient learning. The decoupling of policy gradient and co-imitation modules in our system enables us to leverage the target value function derived from co-imitation to accelerate the learning process, even in the absence of expert demonstrations. The CoRL framework's capability to facilitate inter-agent learning is demonstrated through applications in continuous multi-agent reinforcement learning and learning under partial observability. The name CoRL reflects our ambition to foster a community where agents learn from each other, cooperating to reach a collective understanding. The code for our framework is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/CORL/CoRL.

This paper analyzes two key aspects of Probabilistic Arithmetic Compression: the PAC distance and the probabilistic compression ratio. The PAC distance quantifies the dissimilarity of two data sources by evaluating the expected length difference of compressed data under one source when data is drawn from the other source. The probabilistic compression ratio represents the maximum PAC distance between a source and all possible data sources. We conduct a thorough investigation of these concepts, comparing them to established information-theoretic metrics like the Kullback-Leibler divergence and relative entropy, and examine the impact of code optimization on these metrics.

The intersection of computer vision and neuroscience holds great potential, with hand-centric approaches standing out due to their adaptability to varied camera viewpoints and hand deformations. To demonstrate this, we introduce a hand-centric pipeline that tracks hand interactions with objects and reconstructs 3D shapes of objects from a sequence of unstructured point clouds captured in an uncontrolled environment. Our system begins by designing a compact, efficient hand model that can accurately represent a hand's appearance and underlying joint structure. By projecting this into a 3D Gaussian mixture model and aligning each frame with the previous, we obtain dense hand trajectories suitable for 2D/3D hand tracking. Next, by isolating hand interactions with objects and applying optimized registration, we obtain high-precision object images in a standardized object-centered frame. Our approach yields high-quality object images that enable the construction of high-precision 3D object models. By evaluating our pipeline on 3D/2D tracking and object reconstruction benchmarks, we show that it excels at handling real-world variations in object designs and robustly handles novel objects. The code is available at https://github.com/rotor13/Hand3DGaussian

This study classifies C-groups with a specific Coxeter graph structure - a binary tree with one leaf extended by a chain of nodes connected in succession. It finds all C-groups of solvability class 2 fitting this structure, those with a rank of 4 and an interleaving number of 2, resulting in a list of 12 groups, though this study does not explore the geometric implications for the group types identified.

A research project developed a robot depth adjustment technique that utilizes only visual cues and does not rely on visual markers. This project overcomes the drawbacks of visual-based pose estimation methods that demand excessive computation due to the absence of visual references and visual reliance, which can lead to inaccurate results in the absence of key visual features. By designing an optimized depth camera adjustment algorithm based on 3D reconstruction, rotation, and distortion correction, the project achieved accurate visual reference identification and high-precision end-effector pose estimation with viewing angles of up to 180 degrees and distances of over 50 centimeters. Validation tests demonstrated that this markerless and visual reference-based depth adjustment and end-effector pose estimation technique outperforms visual reliance, with significant improvements in accuracy and accuracy variability when compared to traditional visual reliance, with errors reduced by over 50% and up to 90% respectively. Moreover, computational efficiency was enhanced by approximately 50% due to the elimination of visual feature matching, making the project results promising for the widespread application of robotics and augmented reality.

Identifying and eliminating false positives generated by therapy interference is a critical issue in psychotherapy research and practice, yet there are limited methods available to detect it. This study develops a statistical model known as the K-Nearest-Neighbors Interference Model, which anticipates and compares actual F scale and T scale false positive rates resulting from therapy interference with those predicted by the model. Utilizing randomized clinical trial data that includes both control and therapy interference groups, we evaluate the model's effectiveness. Experimental outcomes show the model can accurately predict and identify the F scale and T scale false positive rates resulting from therapy interference, outperforming existing alternative models. Furthermore, machine learning techniques, specifically decision tree learning, have been found to enhance model efficiency. This advancement enables the model to detect and eliminate control group false positives caused by therapy interference. We also include supplementary data analysis to provide context and insight.

In the context of Neutron stars, we analyze DM annihilation processes involving pseudoscalar interactions, specifically focusing on the final states of neutrinos. We observe that certain DM annihilation outcomes involving lepton pairs are enhanced due to the presence of an lepton-scalar coupling, leading to significant energy releases that could be detected through solar neutrino observations. The presence of electromagnetic or hadronic couplings can also impact the enhancement, sometimes inhibiting it due to final state cancellations. Notably, in preequilibrium Neutron star systems, certain conditions involving distinct pseudoscalar-mediated interactions lead to enhanced emissivity. However, these interactions are less effective in equilibrium systems. The exploration of these potential neutrino emissions in DM annihilation processes could lead to breakthroughs in understanding Dark Matter and Nuclear interactions.

We introduce ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline designed for the efficient measurement of galaxy shapes in large-scale surveys, specifically optimized for the UNIONS/Canada-France-Ile-de-France Survey project. Following the confirmation of a cosmological signal in UNIONS data, we demonstrate the pipeline's capability to deliver reliable shapes for CFI data, accounting for a significant source of 2% cosmic uncertainty in shear measurements. With a targeted approach and thorough validation processes, ShapePipe achieves a 50% reduction in cosmic uncertainty compared to previous measurements for UNIONS/CFIS data. Moreover, we provide a comprehensive description of the pipeline's methodologies and tools, making it adaptable for upcoming major surveys like Euclid and the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, significantly enhancing the measurement of cosmic impact in these projects.

We establish novel arithmetical properties of certain infinite vectors, called Kronecker-Weyl type vectors, and demonstrate the equidistribution of certain related vectors in one dimension. Additionally, we extend a finding by Read and Shelah to a broader context. Our study incorporates concepts from p-adic analysis and automata theory, specifically p-adic valuations of factorials and the behavior of the p-adic partial sums series of the base of a p-adic rational number.

We prove that for five-dimensional complete local rings, being du Bois over the rational numbers is equivalent to being rational. This confirms a conjecture by Ambro in the minimal model program for rational singularities. We also show the same for iterated local complete unions over the rational numbers. This generalizes to other algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero, but our proof is specific to the rational numbers due to its use of Poincaré's theorem on closed differential forms of specific degrees being exact.

We explore a novel implementation of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless model using a magnetic spin array called the spin ice. By adjusting the arrangement of spins in the array, we can either field-cool the system to reach the BEK phase or achieve a driving-insulating state through Magnetic Insulator Exclusion, both leading to evidence of the Thouless viscosity. Furthermore, our research shows that increasing the frequency of a spin array allows for controlled transitions between different magnetic and non-local correlations at low temperatures, enabling the study of spin correlations and Th viscosity at two distinct time scales. Ultimately, our findings highlight the potential for time and space-resolved investigations of phase transitions utilizing precise magnetic control of quantum systems.

We investigate a model of shadow matter consisting of neutrinos and axions.
To address the neutrino oscillation data, we develop a model where right-handed neutrinos interact with active neutrinos through model parameter $\theta$.
This interaction leads to an effective reduction in $\theta$ by factor $(1-\nu_c \bar{\nu}_c)\theta$, resulting in an altered interpretation of neutrino oscillation data in high energy experiments and potential significant enhancements in active-$\sterile$ oscillations.
The model features axion-mediated interactions between $\sterile$ neutrinos, resulting in cross-section scaling with energy as $E^2$.
We analyze collider signatures and axion search implications, finding that small $\theta$ values or large $\sterile$ neutrino mass leads to distinctive predictabilities in collider searches.
On cosmological scales, a portion of the shadow matter can contribute to explaining nearly all neutrino mass-derived energy density in several scenarios, particularly when $\sterile$ neutrino mass is lighter, leading to increased fluctuations in neutrino clumps compared to just-neutrino model predictions.

The concept of rank plays a crucial role in understanding the complexity of quantum circuit computations. Specifically, the dimension of a vector space associated with stabilizer states determines an upper limit on the number of such states that can be reached through a circuit of polynomial size. This has led to the development of techniques for bounding the rank of affinely dependent sets of magic states, which in turn yield improved limits on this dimension. While initial research focused on deriving tight bounds for specific sets of magic states, our investigation expands on this by establishing general, enhanced upper bounds that apply to any magic state set. These new bounds integrate concepts from combinatorial design theory, and when such designs are unavailable, we derive additional limits that rely on established minimum distance properties. The implications of this work are far-reaching, as they restrict the feasible solutions for certain combinatorial problems, resolve long-standing questions about the optimal rank of specific magic state sets, and facilitate the identification of relevant questions about rank that drive future research and development.

This research investigates the application of Complex Essence Model (CEM) in Tsallis Holographic Dark Energy (TDLE) within a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime. We compare the results of the Real Essence Model (REM) and CEM through statefinder analysis and distortion radius calculations. Our study demonstrates that TLEM with CEM effectively describes the expansion history of the universe, accurately predicting observations. Furthermore, CEM's predictions align more closely with data than REM's. In addition, we examine the phase space diagrams and physical properties of TDLE, revealing a difference in its behavior when using CEM versus REM.

Data analysis from four K2 fields of the ongoing LAMOST Time-domain Survey has been published. This major project, set to run for eight years with 283 nights per year, features 10 Drizzle-transformed images per night. Each night's observations include up to 10000 randomly selected objects across two various wavelengths. This study focuses on the data from four K2 fields. Drizzle-transformed images, reduced spectra, and lists of objects per night have been generated and are available online. Our initial findings reveal that the LAMS-TDS significantly enhances our capability to observe various celestial objects such as newly formed stars, variable stars, galaxies with non-steady properties, and transient phenomena. This data showcases the potential benefits of the survey.

In recent years, usage of random number generators based on hardware has increased significantly, yet most RNG designs utilize simple constructions like ring oscillators, memory contents, or threshold voltages in SRAMs. Although these methods are compact and efficient, they often lack the required volume of high-quality random numbers. This paper explores the potential for generating high-volume, hardware-based random numbers using only the supply voltage of SRAMs. To this end, a novel technique known as TuRaN (True Random Number creation using supply voltage underscaling in True circuits) is proposed, which leverages slow down and stochastic behaviors during SRAM cell reading when supply voltage underscaling (VDDSS) is applied. To validate its effectiveness, a detailed 28nm cell library was simulated using HSPICE, and a TuRaN-based RNG architecture was designed and tested using commercial EDA tools and standard test patterns. Experimental results indicate that the proposed TuRaN approach yields a higher bit rate of 129 kbits/sec with significantly lower area and power consumption compared to existing state-of-the-art RNG designs.

A preliminary design of a single-electron resistor switch has been developed using an electron-attached insulating polymer molecule, and a previous study demonstrated its feasibility experimentally with a particular molecule, (perfluorophenyl)6Si (o-DCP). To gain deeper insights, a novel design has been proposed through ab initio and molecular dynamics simulations, focusing on a molecule where a specific site was substituted with a methoxy group, which possesses a higher electron-attached capacity. Notably, the new design exhibits a significant on/off current difference, along with a lower operational voltage compared to the original design, which could lead to more efficient devices.

The scale-separation Feynman parameterization is analyzed from both technical and pedagogical perspectives to gain a deeper understanding of the parameter's role in the amplitude's scale separation. The large and small epsilon expansions of Feynman integrals are examined, along with the relation between these expansions and loop count. The conventional approach to evaluating Feynman integrals involves replacing propagators with a single invariant, effectively separating ultraviolet and infrared divergences. This method is shown to inadvertently discard crucial information about the graph's topological structure and the distribution of momentum within individual loops. A proposed solution addresses this limitation by retaining the scale-separation Feynman parameterization in Feynman integrals, demonstrating its feasibility through a two-loop example. This new approach enables numerical evaluation with finite divergences at each vertex, proving to be beneficial for NNNN helicity amplitude calculations in scattering processes, QCD radiative simulations, and the search for new physics in future colliders.

We introduce a novel approach to solving two-state quantum walk systems by directly expanding their eigenfunctions. This method yields a notable two-component difference equation, which is linked to the four-component eigenvalue equation of the system. Moreover, the coefficients of the expansion are expressed as polynomials in the energy eigenvalue, subject to specific constraints. The success of this approach is demonstrated through application to the free Hamiltonian, which is shown to generate expansions of up to the ninth degree.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The denser sections of the stars are composed of a quark substance, made up of up, down, and a small amount of strange quarks, while the quark mass is influenced by the presence of heavier sigma and omega quarks. In the less dense sections, MIT or NJL models describe the behavior of quark matter, depending on the density level. By combining the equations of state of neutronic and quark stars with the application of the $\beta$-equilibrium condition and chemical continuity, we investigate the mass-radius properties of these hybrid stars. Our analysis reveals that NJL models tend to result in heavier hybrid stars compared to MIT models. Moreover, the inclusion of heavier quarks reduces the maximum mass possible, and this constraint can help distinguish between the validity of these quark interaction models through astronomical observations of massive stars.

The introduction of q-deformation into optomechanical systems offers a novel pathway to explore the impacts of non-standard quantum mechanics on optomechanical dynamics. In this research, a q-deformed optomechanical system consisting of a optomechanical cavity with two coupled resonators is analyzed, dynamically describing the interaction between a directional laser field, a micro-mirror, and two coupled resonators. Notably, Feshbach fields serve as probe fields to investigate optomechanical behavior. It is demonstrated through analytical and numerical methods that optomechanical characteristics can be enhanced within the context of q-deformed dynamics. Furthermore, the clarity and modification of the optomechanical state can be controlled by adjusting the deforming parameter. As the parameter 'q' deviates from unity, the optimal nonstandard quantum mechanics occurs, allowing operational applications of the optomechanical system under the framework of nonstandard quantum mechanics.

A model based on a two-rotor framework has been developed to examine R-negative scissors states, with one rotor representing the nuclear shape and the other, with an infinite moment of inertia, simulating an intrinsic proton rotation. The model's validity was verified by comparing its results to experimental data on some exotic R-negative scissors states and the famous adverse R-positive scissors states found in Ti-44. We suggest that an effective interaction incorporating a Mariposa-like term can accurately reproduce the characteristic characteristics of these adverse R-positive scissors states and obtained results align with experimental findings. We also propose that a Mariposa-like term in the interaction could help in interpreting some exotic R-negative scissors states and that a more detailed analysis of the spectrum in Ti-44 is necessary to confirm the identification of states.

In the realm of ultrathin multilayer materials, particularly oxide films, our focus is on their exceptional magnetic properties and their relevance to unique electronic behaviors. The confinement of magnetic layers within these oxide films enables the study of two-dimensional versions of complex spin and orbital patterns found in their bulk counterparts. These patterns, often characterized by intricate competition and interdependence, are significantly influenced by altered geometries and quantum confinement effects. Consequently, they are particularly susceptible to subtle changes brought about by variations in film thickness. The primary objective of this review is to provide an comprehensive overview of our investigative approaches and findings related to spin and orbital dynamics in ultrathin magnetic film semiconductors and oxides grown on insulating substrates via molecular beam epitaxy. These investigations delve into critical topics such as the impact of lattice mismatch and structural constraints on engineered magnetic systems, the exploitation of unique interface phenomena and unconventional electron behaviors arising from interesting orbital configurations and charge transfers at the epitaxial interface. Additionally, they consider how magnetic and orbital order responds to sophisticated spectroscopic techniques and how external stimuli, such as electric fields and light, can be leveraged to manipulate these patterns and ultimately how they converge into fascinating two-dimensional versions of the phenomena observed in their bulk counterparts.

In an optical setup, where muonic hydrogen atoms are cooled using a combination of a damped optical lattice and a microchip electrode, an unusual statistical behavior emerges. We report on the observation of thermal fluctuations in the number of laser-cooled atoms, an effect predicted earlier theoretically. Our findings reveal a negative correlation in the thermal fluctuations of the atom number, attributed to the presence of the damping mechanism. Additionally, the exponent of the temporal correlation of atom number deviations increases with the rate of damping but decreases as the average atom number increases. We have also extrapolated the results obtained from the indirect damping method to scenarios involving direct damping by substituting the friction coefficient, thereby providing insights into the potential applications of this approach for studying open quantum systems.

Cryptocurrency trading occurs in two primary methods: direct trading at individual exchanges and cross-trading between exchanges. Cross-trading involves transferring to sell orders from one exchange to another, facilitating the trading process. This study analyzes pairwise and higher-order relationships in the global cross-trading network by examining data from 44 major exchanges over a 44-day period, utilizing an orientation to quantify and compare the strength of connections between exchanges. The results reveal a distinct leading exchange and directional patterns in the network, as well as exchanges with no significant relationships and others with higher-order dependencies.

The impact of zero-point motion on the equilibrium properties of tiny water and sulphuric acid droplets is investigated, considering a wide range of temperatures and sizes. The importance of zero-point motion is particularly notable in such nucleation droplets due to the presence of intense hydrogen-bonding vibrations that significantly elevate the zero-point energy. The analysis reveals that accounting for this motion is essential to accurately model nucleation processes in a scenario where quantum effects are predominantly governed by vibrational dynamics.

We establish that the closures of bounded families of group equivariant non-expanding operators, equipped with the bounded Gromov-Hausdorff distance, result in compact compactification spaces. This phenomenon occurs for any infinite group acting on a metric space, leading to various applications. Notably, it is demonstrated that the Heisenberg 3-manifold admits a natural compactification by a single point, while the straight Z^n acts minimally and cocommactly on the compactified Heisenberg 3-space. Moreover, it is shown that the compactification spaces retain rich geometric features, as their fundamental groups are isomorphic to their respective acting groups, possessing properties of being quasi-Fuchsian and having a quasi-isometric equivalence with the stable quasi-length on the group's Cayley graph.

In non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, the Einstein relations connect thermal transport coefficients, however, we show that in systems with short-range interactions, analogues of the Einstein relations are breached. Instead, a thermal counterpart to the Wiedemann-Franz relation is demonstrated, whereas the deeper structure of Einstein relations requires long-range forces, verified by both field-theoretical analysis and numerical investigations.

This study delves into the unexplored connection between various training methods and performance regularizations in neural networks, specifically examining how different training mechanisms influence the model's simplicity. By analyzing complex classification and regression models, we show that models like KNN, KMEANS, and certain gradient-free optimization methods enforce a linear separating hyperplane, similar to linear classifiers. Conversely, the use of gradient-based optimization methods like SGD and Adam has distinct impacts on model complexity and other characteristics, such as the geometric arrangement of decision boundaries and the weight matrix. High row-rank in neural networks is associated with randomized decision boundaries, and this analysis provides an novel perspective on the role of spectral properties in shaping neural network classifiers, offering insights that can guide future research and development in neural network design.

A theoretical framework, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, has been employed to investigate the interaction between $B^0$ and $K^{*0}$ particles with muons, and the transition $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ was analyzed within a specific energy range, between 6 and 8 GeV, to identify possible new physics. By comparing experimental data to the theoretical model, without assuming the Weak interaction, the values of two key parameters, $C_{9}^{(\prime)}$ and $C_{10}^{(\prime)}$, were calculated for different bin sizes. The computed results revealed discrepancies between measurements and predictions that could also be attributed to new physics, where specific coefficients such as $C_{9}^{(\prime)}$, $C_{10}^{(\prime)}$, and $C_{10}^{(\prime)}$ yielded values of $(2.1\pm 0.4)\times10^{-3}$, $-9.0\pm2.2$, and $-9.0\pm2.2$, respectively.

The primary goal of automated essay scoring is to quickly and accurately evaluate the quality of student-written essays.  Over time, the field has moved towards using automated scoring systems that employ Natural Language Processing techniques.  Despite this progress, the quality of scores given by these systems remains a point of debate compared to those from human raters.  One potential area for improvement lies in addressing data limitations, as deep learning models require substantial and diverse datasets to achieve optimal results.  This study explores the application of data enhancement techniques using the Transformer architecture to boost the quality of scores in the essay scoring task.

In the realm of multivariate statistics, there is a crucial need to analyze the relationship between the extreme values of multiple variables. Various methodologies have been proposed to address this requirement. This report aims to consolidate the most significant methods for capturing extreme dependencies and discuss the challenges associated with each approach.

This research examines how intergenerational social mobility could be equitable.
We first establish a fundamental concept, "balanced social mobility," which mandates that a person's social level in their adult life depends solely on their parents' social status, rather than the specific role they play.
To investigate how this principle holds up over time, we develop a dynamic model that accounts for social inequality across different periods and show it's impossible to maintain consistent social progress under these conditions.
However, by incorporating randomness into the model, we discover that adult social status becomes more evenly distributed under certain reasonable assumptions, offering policymakers a framework for evaluating social mobility equity.
Ultimately, the definition of fair social mobility becomes a matter of choosing which probabilities govern the distribution of social roles and how different aspects of social status influence one another across generations.

The symmetry of the wave function for non-relativistic particles is linked to the spin-statistics connection by providing an odd number of factors in the parity argument. These factors establish the connection between spatial location and the wave function's symmetry. To prevent the wave function from being identically zero, the parity of these spatial location factors must compensate for the connection between spin and statistics.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports multi-signature addresses, 
allowing users to opt for a set of signers whose signatures are required to spend 
from that address, among which one must belong to the sender, who then signs the 
transaction and forwards it to the network, acting as the leading node in the 
transaction process. This reduction in required signatures leads to reduced transaction 
sizes and costs, while maintaining complete privacy. Additionally, to minimize 
verification time for recipients, we incorporate Groth arguments instead of Bellare 
arguments, substituting 480+ bytes with just 220 bytes at the expense of adding around 
200 bytes for verification of the sender's identity, thus optimizing verification 
efficiency.

This research explores the concept of space toughness in the context of solving linear systems of equations using the CG and MINRES conjugate gradient methods. Building upon earlier work, we have identified and proved space-toughness lower bounds for these methods under specific matrix patterns. Our study extends existing research by relaxing a critical constraint, thus allowing a more accurate analysis of the memory requirements when solving a linear system of n variables. Additionally, we investigate the space toughness of solving a linear system of equations with an underdetermined matrix under the same constraints. This study also outlines potential avenues for further investigation into space-toughness in the general case and linear systems with specific matrix patterns.

Researchers examined the production of three massive gauge bosons in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level, with an accumulated dataset of 139 fb^-1. The study focused on specific processes involving particular combinations of massive gauge bosons, specifically VBB where V can be either a Z boson or a vector boson. The researchers analyzed various decay patterns of these bosons into electrons and muons, identifying associated leptons and jets while considering potential three boson signals at different invariant mass thresholds. The study found that its findings are consistent with predetermined theoretical predictions without indicating the existence of unusual phenomena. Its most significant results relate to specific scenarios involving total VVV production at a particular threshold and total VBB at an alternative threshold.

In this study, we address the limitations of existing UD Hebrew parsing frameworks, which encompass diverse text types such as news and religious texts. Our research aims to expand the current framework by incorporating an additional corpus of 18k Mafren texts, which we utilize to fine-tune and assess the performance of the already developed UD Hebrew parsing model. Our results demonstrate that fine-tuning substantially enhances data coverage and induces only minor variations in data balance. Furthermore, we found that the model's parameters optimally adapt to the new corpus's characteristics, yielding the best parsing accuracy on both the original and new datasets. Our findings also suggest that the choice of training history and initial parameters significantly impacts the model's performance and should be carefully evaluated. Ultimately, we suggest that the optimized model and parameters serve as a solid foundation for the continued development of the UD Hebrew parsing task.

We investigate the dimension of our new $\varepsilon$-isometric concept and demonstrate its effectiveness by showing that the dimension significantly decreases for incompressible subsets of the incompressibility constant $I(X)$. We also define a specific characteristic for this metric dimension and establish relationships with other scale-invariant concepts. We further demonstrate a property related to商 mappings that results in both an increase and decrease of this dimension.

In the past two decades, the field of system modeling has seen significant growth, with numerous methods being developed and available for diverse applications. However, single researchers or small teams often struggle to establish a consistent approach, resulting in a fragmented knowledge base that hinders knowledge transfer and model evolution. A potential solution to these issues is the adoption of Digital Twins technology, albeit existing solutions tend to be non-interoperable software platforms or websites, limiting collaboration and transparency. This study proposes a novel framework for co-creating Model-Driven Software through the integration of social media platforms. Leveraging social media's inherent network effects, the framework enables the aggregation and seamless sharing of data across multiple contributors, thereby enhancing the reliability of data-driven models by incorporating crowd-sourced feedback. By utilizing a unified interface, the framework facilitates collaborative model development, enabling users to submit issues, report bugs, and provide suggestions directly through social media channels.

This study explores the performance limits of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with interdependent degree patterns in the presence of a binary deletion channel. We derived a capacity function, setting an upper bound on achievable rates. Numerical results show that this upper bound is close to LDPC code performance. We then developed LDPC codes with degrees following Poisson distributions, achieving capacity接近ness by within one bit. For a narrow deletion probability range, we developed LDPC ensembles at one bit per capacity. We also examined finite length performance and found codes with skewed degree patterns outperform those with degrees concentrated at two and three. Notably, these optimized ensemble codes showed significant gains, up to 0.62 bits, over traditional LDPC ensembles.

A predictive filter for discrete-time linear systems with delayed control input is developed within the System Level Synthesis framework. This new constraint, arising from all possible trajectories of the closed loop system, enables the creation of novel constraints over predictive states, thus expanding the set of admissible predictive states. An optimal cost function state-dependent and quadratic in nature is created, which allows for the optimization of the predictive state variance through an efficient quadratic program. Predictive safety constraints over the predictive state can be formulated directly from the novel admissible set of predictive states thus expanding the set of admissible predictive states. This new constraint, which considers all possible trajectories, leads to the identification of the minimal set of initial conditions that能保证系统安全. An attractive characteristic of this filter is its offline computability. Furthermore, when applied to a flexible link manipulator with a delayed torque input, the proposed filter proves its robustness in handling difficult control conditions.

We've discovered a new flaw in the standard quantum key distribution data processing methods which reduces overall key rates but fails to prevent side-channel attacks targeting phase randomization. Our attack targets systems employing partial phase randomization by exploiting the insufficiently randomized phase, achieving higher success rates than in fully randomized systems. We developed a computational model to simulate this attack and demonstrate its feasibility. We propose enhancing the security of QKD by either fully randomizing phases or implementing post-selection techniques.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have revolutionized the development of various AI applications across multiple domains. However, investigating the underlying mechanisms driving these models poses a significant challenge. In this study, we employ the 175-billion-parameter Chinese pre-trained language model, ChatGLM2, to examine the impact of pretraining corpora on in-context learning performance. By using controlled datasets, we assess the model's ability to learn in-context without updating its weights through various ablation experiments, analyzing datasets of varying sizes, domains, and linguistic features. We discover that pretraining on diverse, high-quality, domain-specific corpora is crucial in enhancing the model's in-context learning capabilities, particularly in scenarios where the target task data is limited and the pretraining process is confined to non-domain-specific, general corpora. Notably, our results indicate that enhancing the linguistic characteristics of pretraining data, such as writing standards, can significantly boost in-context learning outcomes. In summary, our research sheds light on two key aspects of pretraining corpora that are essential for optimizing in-context learning: domain relevance and domain linguistic characteristics.

To investigate the effect of radiative instability on the structure of the intracluster medium (ICM) in galaxy clusters, we performed numerical simulations based on radiative cooling and the growth of cold clouds. Our simulations incorporated the influence of cooling processes in the ICM, the growth of turbulence, and the development of cold clouds. Our results demonstrate that these effects collectively contribute to a significant increase in cloud mass as well as mass growth rates. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that the growth of cold clouds is strongly affected by magnetic fields and thermal conduction. Specifically, aligned magnetic fields and high thermal conduction rates suppress the growth of cold clouds, while randomly oriented magnetic fields have a minimal impact on cloud mass. Our study also revealed that the morphologies of clouds are strongly influenced by magnetic fields and cooling rates, with randomly oriented magnetic fields promoting elongated cloud shapes and randomly oriented fields, and highly aligned magnetic fields tend to form rounder clouds.

The term "elegance" in particle physics refers to a symmetrical relationship between particles that are counterparts to each other. This document explores the minute discrepancies observed between elegant particles, specifically mesons, which contradict the anticipated beautiful parity conservation. A series of experiments conducted in 2012 have confirmed that the difference between these particles is quantifiable and measurable. To better understand this phenomenon, theories have been proposed to explain why the magnitude of these discrepancies varies, suggesting potential underlying causes.

The research investigates how superstring theory's scattering cross sections relate to its high-energy behavior properties. Specifically, it demonstrates that the generalized Gross conjecture holds true for all bosonic hard string interactions in the context of superstring theory.

As the date approaches for the deployment of the first 5G networks, it is crucial to address a critical challenge - the administration and upkeep of the newly created 5G cellular networks. Given the substantial size and intricacy anticipated of these networks, traditional management methods are unlikely to be feasible. Thus, an innovative and effective framework for 5G network management needs to be established to ensure optimal performance, troubleshoot issues, and maintain configuration settings of the network's core components. This has necessitated the development of the Network Exposure and Management System (NEMS), which provides operators with the necessary tools to effectively manage 5G networks. This review focuses on the fundamental principles of 5G network administration, explores various strategies for 5G management, and highlights the most promising approaches for operational management, troubleshooting, and configuration tasks. Additionally, we review the NEMS framework that enables the implementation of these management procedures.

State-of-the-art voice synthesis models rely on extensive datasets of available audio samples, but a significant number of individuals do not have a available recording of their own voice. The elements that define a person's voice can also be explored through speech analysis, and these aspects could be leveraged in cases where a person lacks an available voice sample. A novel approach called uVRSS (unverified Voice Resource Synthesis) aims to overcome this limitation by enabling voice synthesis for individuals whose voices have not been previously captured. The proposed method involves breaking down texts into smaller units based on how the human ear perceives speech, and these units are then used to train a neural network to learn voice characteristics from available data. The effectiveness of uVRSS will be evaluated by comparing the synthesized speech to that of the target individual and to a pre-existing audio recording of their speech. The results of this research will significantly contribute to the fields of multilingual and zero-resource voice synthesis.

We approach the challenge of moving through complex environments with obstacles by employing a step-wise strategy that involves multiple planning stages. Beginning with a simple and non-convex method for finding a general path, we refine it using an advanced technique for approximating its properties. We then integrate this approximation with a more complex planner to find an optimal trajectory while considering the effects of dynamic forces. To make our planner efficient, we develop a method for rapidly estimating properties of the environment's obstacles by analyzing how we move through them, ensuring that we maintain a high level of accuracy while minimizing computational cost. Our algorithm demonstrates that our planner is able to find optimal motions efficiently, even in cases where a simple random approach is not sufficient, and that our planner is able to adapt to different scales of computation without losing accuracy.

PBQC is a crucial concept in quantum information processing and the study of open quantum systems. Unfortunately, current methods for determining if two quantum states can be transformed into each other probabilistically are limited to specific scenarios, such as when the states are diagonal. To bridge this gap, we've developed a universally applicable criterion for probabilistic transformation of arbitrary quantum states. Our new criterion exceeds existing results and reduces to a well-known condition when the states are diagonal. Furthermore, we've combined this with a relevant result to create a complete set of necessary and sufficient stochastic transformation criteria. In addition, we've tested our model on a wide range of non-diagonal states and found it to be accurate even in extreme cases.

The motion of a liquid in a cup while walking resembles a chaotic pendulum undergoing a series of small variations in acceleration. To understand the movement of the liquid, the acceleration can be modeled as driving the pendulum within a range of frequencies, and the goal is to predict the resulting oscillations in a way that explains the characteristic swinging sensation experienced while carrying a cup of liquid.

The Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (D-DSGD) algorithm has become the go-to choice for networked machine learning due to its robustness in the face of data discrepancies between various network nodes. Nevertheless, the sensitivity of D-DSGD to outliers in data gradients becomes a significant problem, particularly when D-DSGD is applied to decentralized stochastic learning across networks with various characteristics. This issue motivates researchers to develop a more resilient D-DSGD variant that can effectively cope with heterogeneous network environments. In response, we introduce a new algorithm, DR-DSGD, which is a distributionally robust extension of D-DSGD, capable of withstanding the influences of heterogeneous network settings. Mathematically, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is an $\ell_2$-norm ball regularized version of D-DSGD, and that it can guarantee a distributionally robust machine learning solution for a range of pre-established uncertainty levels. Furthermore, we show that the proposed algorithm's design can be derived from a game-theoretic perspective by formulating it as a minimax optimization problem. Numerical experiments confirm that DR-DSGD can significantly outperform D-DSGD in terms of robustness while maintaining high accuracy.

We utilize the BDNK relativistic fluid dynamic equation to explore the hydrodynamic attractor in relativity, comparing solutions obtained through different numerical techniques. The effectiveness of the method using the tln(εbar) variables is shown, enabling a range of universal, dimensionless functions to describe the system's evolution across varying initial energy densities and relaxation times. Furthermore, we investigate the formation of particles within this framework.

The origin of low-velocity outflows from young stars remains unclear, and research suggests that high-velocity jets produced by magnetic processes could contribute significantly. Our goal is to investigate whether these high-velocity jets can drive low-velocity outflows, and we used 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model this phenomenon. Our study utilized the ENZO code and employed two initial magnetic field configurations: one where field lines were aligned with the rotation axis and another where they were spiraling.
