When simulating a single phase, our results showed that regardless of the magnetic field configuration, low-velocity outflows were not produced. However, incorporating dust and cosmic rays into the model yielded mixed outcomes. Although the alignment of magnetic field lines with the rotation axis led to low-velocity outflows under specific conditions, incorporating cosmic rays rendered this scenario physically implausible due to the requirement of an external particle acceleration source. On the other hand, when simulating a multi-phase model that accounted for the role of radiation pressure in molecular gas and scattering of magnetic electrons in a partially ionized medium, our low-velocity outflow model achieved physical feasibility.

This study develops an equilibrated control strategy for constrained nonlinear systems that adaptively balances stability and invariance within the system's feasible region. The proposed controller ensures the system remains inside a specific bounded area by adjusting its position relative to that bounded area. What makes this controller unique is its ability to optimize performance near the bounded area and retreat for stability as it moves away from that bounded area. This study ensures and verifies the robustness of the proposed controller in keeping the system within the feasible region. The proposed controller's value lies in its simultaneous focus on maintaining system invariance and enhancing its performance.

Orbital resonances of satellites present significant challenges in orbit determination and anomaly identification. The solar radiation pressure can also induce SSRs under specific orbital conditions, although they are rarely encountered in Earth orbits. The current study employs an analytical framework based on Draper's epoch ephemeris elliptical elements model and supports these findings with numerical simulations using STK software. By comparing these approaches, the research defines precise analytical criteria for detecting solar resonance. The investigation specifically focuses on the three primary types of solar resonance: CS_SR, CSR_S, and CSR_SR. The analysis confirms that resonance thresholds derived from the elliptical elements model align closely with those obtained through numerical methods, highlighting the necessity of accounting for resonance periods. The research demonstrates that certain resonance types can undergo period inversions depending on the chosen evaluation zone. For low-inclination orbits, the analysis shows that DRAPER matches the numerical approach in predicting the boundary of the solar resonance CSR_S, while identifying a more outer boundary compared to the STK method. For high-inclination orbits, the analytical model identifies a boundary more inclusive than the STK's assessment for the solar resonance CSR_S, illustrating the value of analytical evaluation in identifying the onset of solar resonance phenomena.

A model for tightly-bonded solids derived from first-principle theories exhibits measure invariance when the measure relies on lattice sites rather than individual electrons. Furthermore, introducing electron correlations does not alter this measure invariance. From a theoretical standpoint, this feature suggests distinct advantages for tightly-bonded models over more commonly-used freely-bonded models, such as the standard Density Functional Theory (DFT) method. Notably, physical properties calculated using these tightly-bonded models align closely with both freely-bonded and DFT predictions, while adhering to an enhanced measure invariance principle.

This research introduces the novel task of estimating the identity, geometry, and configuration of a specific object using either 2D semantic keypoints on that object or just some of its relevant keypoints. To achieve this, we've developed a model that learns to identify these features from unstructured data, allowing us to predict the object's position and shape using only a few relevant keypoints on either 2D semantic images or 3D point clouds. To test our model's effectiveness, we've created a new benchmark dataset that includes difficult examples of categories with many variations. Our results show that training on 2D images yields better outcomes than training on 3D point clouds.

This study introduces a set of iterative procedures to produce confidence intervals 
for parameters of a Cauchy distribution based on order statistics from samples 
of varying sizes. The findings indicate that certain intervals derived using these 
procedures exceed the specified coverage probability, while others fall below the 
pro specified level. The results show significant improvement in performance 
for larger sample sizes. An additional extension of these methods involves choosing 
the interval based on the least squared difference of order statistics.

A new statistical method is developed to calculate the required sample size for complex clinical trials known as interactive basket trials. These trials evaluate multiple patient groups with the same treatment, and "borrow" statistical information from each other to improve accuracy. The proposed approach uses an interactive multivariate normal model for different subsets and determines effective borrowing based on the similarity of their response distributions. Through extensive simulations, the new method demonstrates accurate results in estimating sample sizes and "borrowing" amounts, and real-world data, including a trial called COMPASSION, shows that similar, smaller studies can provide valuable insights for each other.

High-precision motion systems are subject to various uncertainties including dynamic interactions, system uncertainties and disturbances, which significantly hinder their performance in the presence of equilibrium position errors.  For systems with multiple degrees of freedom, these influences can be mitigated through sequential loop tightening, a strategy designed to simplify the system.  Nevertheless, conventional sequential loop tightening often falls short in moving systems due to limitations such as difficulty in achieving exact loop separation, restricted plant sensitivity restrictions and the need for time-domain simulation.  In this research, sequential loop tightening is enhanced for linear parameter-varying systems by formulating loop-closing conditions in the form of linear matrix inequalities.  As a result, loop-closing gains can be efficiently computed through convex optimization.  Moreover, a new criterion is proposed to ensure the satisfaction of sensitivity restrictions without the necessity of calculating specific frequency responses.  Moreover, LMI constraints are derived to guarantee the loop-closing performance in a data-driven manner.  Ultimately, the proposed method's feasibility and effectiveness are demonstrated through successful application to a laboratory-scale dual-gyroscopic suspended platform system.

Our research centers around the critical real-world alignment challenge of partially observable partial shapes, extending traditional partial-to-partial alignment that has numerous applications in robotics and computer vision. We identify two significant obstacles in this challenge: hidden surface information and connected global context. To address these challenges, we introduce a reusable module called the Repeated Progress-Network (PRNet), which aligns available surface data while recovering and integrating hidden surface information through a simplified, repeatable structure. Notably, PRNet demonstrates superior generalization capabilities and aligns multiple complete shapes after learning from just one complete shape. Our research further reveals that PRNet excels in handling varied pose configurations and robustly performs even with high levels of visible surface data and varying camera viewpoints.

A group that possesses an infinite number of conjugacy classes is classified as R-infinite. We examine the condition of being R-infinite in quotient groups derived from d-hyperbolic HNN-extensions of nilpotent groups, specifically focusing on the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar group $G_\infty$. We establish a criterion for a quotient group of $G_\infty$ to exhibit the R-infinite characteristic, and then apply this criterion to determine the R-infinite characteristic in certain nilpotentizations of $G_\infty$.

The intention is to investigate the breakdown of the electroweak vacuum at a lower energy threshold, specifically within the context of the Standard Model. Although the exact mechanism is unclear, various theoretical models suggest that new physics could emerge within the range of 1-100 times the current LHC energy capabilities. To explore this idea, a framework for selecting the most suitable collider is proposed within a multi-stage strategy. Initially, precise measurements of the Higgs boson are required. Following this, the most promising collider is selected for searching for the threshold of instability, based on its reach in exploring very small production cross-sections of Standard Model processes. Ultimately, if the threshold for vacuum breakdown is discovered to be beyond the energy capabilities of any collider within a feasible timeframe, a theoretical deduction that the proposed scenario of metastability is flawed is inevitable. Consequently, this would necessitate reevaluating model parameters or considering revisions to the Standard Model.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments in physics and chemistry using an approach grounded in optimal control theory. The method seeks to find the most accurate description of a system's evolution by matching predicted and actual experimental observations across multiple time points. Formulating this problem within a framework of optimal control problems enables leveraging existing robust optimization algorithms that excel at handling noisy, imperfect data. The solution to this problem yields a sequence of state estimates at discrete time steps, from which a continuous trajectory can be reconstructed using pieces from the basis functions involved in the optimization. The approach is tested successfully on synthetic data from real quantum experiments, demonstrating its ability to reconstruct the trajectory of a quantum state despite noise. Additionally, the method proves versatile for a range of contexts beyond the specific example provided.

The spatial distribution profiles of the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons are calculated and analyzed, with a substantial part of their charge radii attributed to the sea quark's angular momentum. This profile is determined using the Bethe-Salpeter wave function approach, which also facilitates an examination of the influence of the bound quark's mass on the meson mass and distribution profile.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the behavior of a function and its Fourier transform in specific domains. The descriptions we present utilize a combination of weighted $L^p$-spaces and domains defined by exponential decay. The non-triviality of these spaces is demonstrated under various conditions, specifically when p is less than 2, a certain conjugate value of q, or in the case of shrinking domains. The non-triviality under these conditions is derived from the uncertainty principle and shares similarities with results obtained by Beckner and Tao. The weighted nature of these spaces enables the analysis of Toeplitz operators to preserve specific properties, and we apply this approach to examine the Toeplitz operator with the exponential multiplication operator and determine the conditions under which it is bounded.

Instance segmentation is a well-established task for trained models, however, the presence of unlabelled modalities significantly hampers this process due to a lack of direct observation and multi-modal correlations. Existing methods relying on visual cues prove ineffective in this scenario, leading researchers to develop novel approaches. We introduce a Cyclic Division Generative Adversarial Network (CD-GAN) based method for identifying unlabelled modalities within a given image without prior training. CD-GAN distinguishes between visible and unvisible parts of an image, enabling the generation of images that accurately represent their actual appearance, thus enabling a generator to distinguish these parts effectively. We apply a discriminative network to evaluate model performance on real-world images and conduct experiments on the NuItSe dataset to highlight the challenges posed by unlabelled modalities and outperform baseline methods.

A well-regarded RNN-based model, the LSTM, has proven effective for sequential data analysis and prediction. Although this RNN model has demonstrated remarkable results in numerical data processing, its direct application to handling high-dimensional categorical data has been limited. In our study, we have addressed this gap by adapting the RNN architecture for CVP (Customer Value Proposition) data, which consists of discrete, non-numeric features. By combining a novel mapping of categorical data with the RNN's predictive capabilities and incorporating an analysis of action probabilities, we have achieved a notable improvement in prediction accuracy. Our methodology has been tested and validated using a comprehensive dataset, which we have developed in collaboration with business stakeholders for the CVP data. Our results have demonstrated the RNN's effectiveness in handling categorical data and providing valuable, real-time insights that can be leveraged for strategic decision-making.

A remarkable UV continuum emission was observed during AD Leo's Great Flare on April 12th 1985, a UV shift of over 1 Angstrom at 3 Angstrom in its decay phase. This study utilizes a theoretical model to investigate the flare's dynamics, examining simulations across multiple wavelengths. Through comparison with observed data, significant insights into the flare's covariances and energy distribution have been obtained. The analysis confirms that NA and FS processes played a role in the flare's development. Had a beam-like motion occurred, this model would have accurately predicted the observed X-rays and UV continuum shift.

We explore the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2 manifolds or maps, using an approach that employs metric perturbation methods. Our method can also be applied to analyze the deformation theory of Hitchin sections in symplectic surfaces.

A bounded composition operator $C_\phi$ on the Hardy space $H^2$ is said to $C_\psi$-normal if it commutes with its adjoint under composition with the weighted composition operator $C_\psi$. Under certain conditions on the linear fractional transformation $\psi$, a sufficient and constructive condition for the weighted composition operator $C_\psi$ to be closed $C_\phi$-normal in terms of its coefficients is provided. In addition, under specific constraints on the parameters of $C_\psi$, it is shown that a closed $C_\phi$-normal operator exists which does not admit a closed invariant invariant subspace.

This paper builds upon its previous work to examine the properties of large p-core p' partitions, where p is a prime number. We investigate the high-order growth of the number of such partitions, denoted as $a(n,p)$, where n is greater than or equal to 0. We establish that the count of these partitions can be modeled by a random walk on the additive residue graph of the set of non-negative integers and shows that the primary eigenvalue determines the main characteristic of this random walk. We then utilize this model to confirm a conjecture proposed by Krattenthaler and Olsson regarding the asymptotic behavior of these partitions, where the count is shown to increase or decrease in a specific pattern based on the value of n. We extend our research by also counting p-core p' partitions with a given largest part.

Neural networks that handle 3D data in its raw form are in great demand for a variety of 3D tasks. However, most current frameworks are designed to work with grid-structured input, which can lead to suboptimal performance and significant memory usage due to the need for numerous repeated calculations to achieve grid alignment. On the other hand, handling unstructured point cloud data directly is more computationally efficient but comes with a challenging optimization landscape. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new technique that learns a consistent and efficient data structure from multiple views of 3D scenes. This framework starts by converting unstructured point clouds into a new type of representation that can be used for various applications. We then introduce a new training approach that maximizes the shared information between the original unstructured data and the new representation, which also ensures that various views are treated as different rotations of the same scene. We've tested our framework on numerous datasets and found it surpasses existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy and computational efficiency.

We introduce a new medium access framework for frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar networks and evaluate its underlying access protocols. FMCW signals are utilized in various applications, such as autonomous driving and the Internet of Things, to gather proximity data of objects within a specified range. To facilitate the sharing of this capability, we have developed a common interface for configuring and operating FMCW radars, which includes implementing a medium access control protocol suitable for radar networks. This paper presents a proposed ALOLA protocol, which is based on the slotted ALOHA principle and specifically tailored to accommodate the operational constraints of FMCW radars. To assess the performance of our proposed protocol, we conducted simulations utilizing a HIL setup with actual FMCW transceivers adhering to the AALISA standard. Furthermore, we evaluate an alternative protocol, which leverages a more conventional CSMA approach but requires significant modifications to accommodate AALISA constraints, which we refer to as MCSMA. Through these evaluations, we are able to compare the efficacy of our proposed access protocols under varied system conditions, ultimately identifying Slotted ALOHA, as implemented in the AALISA standard, as the most effective solution for maximizing system capacity and operational reliability within FMCW radar networks.

Examine the two-photon absorption two-photon coupling process in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiment from a spectral perspective, where four-photon states emerge in the form of entangled beams. Employing the Hodgkinson method, four-photon density operators are developed and analyzed in terms of quantum correlations. Numerical computations of the quantum correlations demonstrate that the outputs from each detector exhibit inverse behaviors. Additional experiments, such as measuring the average photon numbers and calculating the G22 correlation function, indicate that quantum correlations in MH and MH' outcomes display inverse behaviors when considering a narrow spectral range. However, the G22 correlation function's calculation at a wider spectral range indicates that MH and MH' produce the same result, and MQ and QM produce different results.

We develop an local structure description for the elliptic cohomology of complex
vector spaces CP(V) under the action of V. This is achieved by establishing a correspondence
between the C^T-local elliptic cohomology theories of CP(V) and the finitely presented
C^T spectra associated with the Weyl group of V. This relationship enables us to identify the
elliptic cohomology theories for the complex Grassmannians as specific instances of this framework.

Temporal knowledge graph reasoning involves predicting unobserved facts within time-sensensitive graphs. Recent advancements have made significant progress on this task, primarily focusing on relation representation. However, these methods are limited by their reliance on specific models, such as neural or graph models. Our proposed framework addresses this gap and offers a unified solution for temporal KGR from various representation models. We introduce a low-rank representation technique for time-sensational relations that captures their dynamic characteristics effectively. Furthermore, we define a novel entropy-based signal to quantify the influence of low-rank representations on target facts. This entropy indicator serves to evaluate the quality of target facts and facilitates the identification of knowledge graph events. We conducted comprehensive experiments on two real-world datasets and seven types of representation models to validate our assumptions. Our results demonstrate that the model aggregation method surpasses individual learning in scenarios where multiple knowledge graph representation models are employed, ultimately leading to a state-of-the-art performance.

In the context of Bouldering AI, particularly for identifying Bouldering Moves, the influence of the ground sound on the detection of cliffhangers and bouldering moves needs to be investigated. We conducted an experiment to assess how removing ground sound affects Bouldering AI performance on cliffhangers and bouldering moves. Our findings indicate that eliminating ground sound diminishes the success rate of cliffhangers and lowers the accuracy of bouldering moves, but the impact on bouldering moves is less pronounced.

A demonstration of Bell nonlocality without inequalities does not rely solely on perfect correlations between shared resources, as illustrated in this paper. We show through mathematical analysis that a single nonlocal box's worth of common randomness is sufficient, under specific conditions. These conditions are met in our setup, allowing us to derive a reliable outcome from just one trial. We achieved this by examining a relationship among three-bits that exhibits nonlocality in itself, despite local equivalent distributions appearing fully determined by marginal distributions. We apply this finding to real-world demonstrations using noisy channels.

The flat line phenomenon observed in models of replica symmetry breaking can be characterized as the precise annulment between energetic gains achieved through replica symmetry breaking and the cost incurred due to disorder fluctuations resulting from replica symmetry. A newly developed framework for understanding the flat line is presented, utilizing an infinite system of coupled "spin glasses" representing replicas. Through this construction, replica symmetry breaking is redefined as a form of hierarchical organization among these spin glasses. Empirical results from one-dimensional and two-dimensional classical Ising models, as well as their 1D and 2D variants featuring both kinetic and geometric constraints, demonstrate that replica symmetry breaking arises from distinct mechanisms. In kinetic constrained models, it is associated with energy terms canceling out, whereas in geometrically constrained models, it is associated with fluctuation costs being nullified.

A thorough examination was conducted to investigate the impact of hydrogen's impact on the superconducting properties of sulfur and carbon-based compounds by employing a hybrid approach that integrates ab-initio molecular dynamics with the Stoner-Weyl theory and Ginzburg-Landau model applications. It was discovered that incorporating hydrogen into the sulfur and carbon-based superconductors led to diminished critical temperatures. Specifically, incorporating hydrogen into the sulfur superconductor caused the loss of its superconducting properties upon heating to 150 Kelvin, while incorporating hydrogen into the carbon-based superconductor also resulted in a decline in its critical temperature. These findings demonstrate that hydrogen's incorporation into these materials negatively affects their superconducting properties. Consequently, in compounds suspected of exhibiting high-temperature superconductivity with exceptional behavior, the presence of hydrogen should be eliminated to achieve the highest possible critical temperature. Moreover, this research offers the Stoner-Weyl theory as a highly effective means for investigating the impact of hydrogen's presence on the superconducting properties of various materials.

Run allocation, a long-standing issue in operating systems, refers to the optimal placement of contiguous segments of processes, a concept known as "runs," within the memory. The traditional approach, based on the assumption of uniform runs distribution, has been the standard for decades. However, the recent introduction of the flattened run allocation problem has revealed that this assumption is flawed, as not all runs have equal distribution. The challenge now is to develop an efficient allocation algorithm that takes the varying run lengths of processes into account and minimizes the objective function specifically identified for this problem. The solution is complicated by the absence of precise run length information before the first run is processed. A new allocation policy, adapted from the best-fit algorithm and specifically designed to accommodate the flat run allocation problem, has been developed. Thorough analysis and simulations have demonstrated the effectiveness of this solution in comparing favorably to other proposed approaches.

Research has revealed similarities, suggesting that the spectral properties of the arithmetic surface derived from the catemap function are governed by chaos. Specifically, we demonstrate a correlation between the charmability of the catemap function and the stiffness of the associated arithmetic surface. We also show that the stiffness and the spectral dimension of the surface are interconnected. Furthermore, we state that the stiffness, the spectral dimension, and the Lyapunov exponent can all be expressed as functions of the catemap function's multiplication factor.

Modern self-driving cars rely on systems that can continue operating in the event of failures, a concept known as fail-operational awareness. Establishing that these systems function correctly when unforeseen faults occur is a challenging process that necessitates validating complex real-world behaviors within a controlled environment. To achieve this, researchers have developed a fail-operational awareness framework for autonomous driving systems, which they then verify using formal validation. In this instance, the team verifies a component of this framework, responsible for detecting faults in the system's perception and localisation systems, using the Isabelle/HOL theorem prover. By incorporating advanced logic within the Isabelle library, the team achieves a high degree of formal confidence in the correctness of the detection logic.

This research explores a method for categorizing dynamical systems based on the potential impact of their behavior. The proposed method uses data-driven techniques to identify similar evolution paths in dynamical systems, without pre-defined features or pre-processed data. By applying these techniques to various benchmark cases, the method successfully finds distinct states of the systems that have a significant effect on their future behavior and reveals new insights into the underlying dynamics of the systems. The research also demonstrates that the method can discover novel types of boundary surfaces in multi-dimensional systems and provides a framework for understanding the potential future behavior of data-driven dynamical systems without requiring prior knowledge of their governing equations.

Infinitesimal calculus, as formulated by Leibniz, has been the subject of mathematical analysis for over three centuries. In contrast, our paper aims to present the original methods of infinitesimal calculus as they were practiced by Leibniz and his contemporaries. The account is structured around three key principles that underpin infinitesimal reasoning: a specific concept of a function, a fundamental property of its variations, and the infinitesimal principle which serves as the foundation for a wide range of calculations. The adoption of the function concept, the infinitesimal principle, and the transformation of variations into finite quantities enabled the development of a comprehensive theory of infinitesimal quantities, which formed the basis for a unified framework of calculation.

Using two approaches, we calculate the HI 21-cm signal for large-scale structures and employ a fast simulation to estimate the HI 21-cm brightness temperature. The simulations take into account the clumping of baryons and the interplay between reionization and structure formation. The predictions from our simulations align with existing research on large-scale HI 21-cm signals, including those produced by the HI intensity mapping technique. The simulations demonstrate the impact of foreground removal on these signals, revealing a long-tail distribution that decreases at lower frequencies and exhibits significant variations based on redshift. To minimize these variations, we suggest restricting the signal analysis to specifically selected redshift ranges.

Our analysis has specific objectives. The primary goal is to demonstrate through specific examples that the independence of the Planck constant, the speed of light, and the permutation group elements is not mutually exclusive. The secondary objective is to show that the temporal or spatial separation of the experiments has no impact on the outcomes, addressing the concerns raised by Bell's inequality violations.

Recommender systems are essential in guiding users to the most relevant documents within the vast expanse of the internet. Various types of recommender systems have been developed, each addressing different types of user needs. In this study, we explore the benefits of combining multiple approaches to creating recommender systems. By comparing a document-context-focused method utilizing a Document Context Awareness (DCA) model with a behavior-based method employing collaborative filtering, we demonstrate that an integrated system outperforms individual techniques in terms of recall at k. Our recommendations for designing a high-quality integrated recommender system are provided, along with examples of applications where such systems are applicable.

The optimization problem of determining the optimal theoretical performance of a matrix is explored more deeply by investigating its theoretical limit known as "optimality" within a broader context of randomness. A theoretical benchmark for achieving this optimal performance in random matrices is represented by "type B openness," which signifies the optimal performance is the maximum possible in the realm of random matrices sharing the same empirical spectral distribution. We demonstrate that in the case of random matrices following a Gaussian distribution, achieving optimal performance is equivalent to achieving free randomness among all independent perturbation matrices. Additionally, for random matrices with real symmetric properties, both type B openness and free randomness can be preserved under certain transformations. Certain real-world applications include the analysis of nearest neighbor nonbacktracking matrices in sparsely connected networks and the performance limits of random matrices with real entries.

The concept of "observing timed properties" addresses how to verify whether a specific property holds true for all possible system behaviors starting from an initial state. Traditionally, this has been studied within the context of non-deterministic, time-sensitive systems. However, this paper revisits the topic in light of recent findings. It proposes solutions for both deterministic and non-deterministic systems, and demonstrates that for a particular class of non-deterministic systems, the observing process can be efficiently modeled, even with an exponential state increase.

The decay process $ \bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta $ near the $ \pi^0 \eta $ threshold can be investigated, considering that the primary contributions come from intermediate $ a_0(980) $ and $ f_0(980) $ states which couple with varying strengths to the $ J/\psi $ and light meson vector meson dominance. A formula has been developed for calculating the transition form factors linked to these resonances and the decay amplitude of $ \bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980) $ and $ \bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980) $. Our research finds that the transition form factors for $ a_0(980) $ and $ f_0(980) $ exhibit virtual singularities due to the complex nature of their masses and widths. As a result, significant loop corrections occur at both production and resonant stages, leading to a substantial, around 50%, reduction in transition probabilities. Moreover, the coupling of $ a_0(980) $ with the $ J/\psi $ and $ a_0(980) $'s real coupling to the $ K K $ channel contributes notably to this channel. Conversely, when considering the couplings between the transition and the link between the resonances and the quark components

The GRAVITY observing mode on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer utilizes four single-point detectors to record the interferometric and spectral information. A unique feature is the use of a 4-pixel grating, which creates four distinct images of the source with varying wavelengths. A gravity camera is a specialized detector that collects signals from all four detectors and integrates them into a customized image using software. This paper presents the characterization results of the gravity camera and its performance in real-time, which has been validated through various astronomical observations.

The k-center problem involves finding k points within a metric space to minimize the maximum distance from any point in the space to its nearest center point. We analyze the dimensionality of the space in terms of exponential vs polynomial approximation algorithms for this problem. We introduce a new dimension, called freeway dimension, which provides upper bounds on the number of points required to certain geometric properties. Specifically, we show that for spaces with a certain freeway dimension, a small number of points can establish a large diameter with a specific radius constraint, which implies a more accurate approximation for the 3-k-center problem. However, we also prove that a lower bound on the number of points needed to establish a certain doubling constant for a specific geometric structure, which gives upper bounds on doubling constant for certain geometric structures.
In this study, the authors focus on the uniqueness of entire functions in the context of their p-th order differential operators.

We investigate solving systems of multivariate polynomials, over a prime field with a large number of elements, of degrees d1 through dr with at least one non-zero solution. Our investigation builds upon an existing algorithm by Fournier et al., which successfully solves a system where all equations are degree d, by utilizing a probabilistic approach even in the presence of errors up to (r-1)(d/2) - O(1). Through an optimized polynomial basis, we demonstrate the ability to tolerate even more errors while decreasing the computational workload. Moreover, our analysis leads to an early termination method, which significantly reduces the time complexity under favorable conditions. Ultimately, our work yields an improved probabilistic algorithm with a time complexity of O~(rdd^ndn), surpassing the previous best deterministic algorithm's complexity of O~(rd^ndn).

The growth of quantum communication technology is pivotal in advancing secure data transfer. We have developed a secure communication method based on quantum states of light within an on-demand package emission system involving a diamond doped with nitrogen atoms and a highly reflective optical cavity. By utilizing a parity-eigenstate embedded within the diamond's quantum energy levels, we can efficiently generate single photons with deterministic accuracy while preserving quantum key distribution (QKD) security standards. Moreover, our designed protocol mitigates the inherent randomness of the process, ensuring a long-term security guarantee for quantum communication needs.

A simplified model is developed to describe the thermodynamic properties of an equilibrium gas consisting of neutral atoms, ions, and electrons. Using the law of mass action in its exponential form, we derive precise analytical expressions for key variables such as density and internal energy. These equations are then applied to calculate temperature-dependent energy and specific heat for certain alkali metals. The results show that energy and specific heat exhibit complex behavior that cannot be easily predicted, including non-intuitive trends in the number of particles and properties of ions. This approach offers a fundamental understanding of how temperature influences the ionization of particular alkali metals. The model is particularly useful for engineering designs involving low-pressure systems, we elucidated that the equilibrium state of an ideal gas is achieved when its entropy attains a maximum value. This leads to a simplified model for ionization in a particular type of alkali metal.

Our study investigates the impact of chiral asymmetry in the fermionic vacuum on the spectrum of vector mesons. We utilize the N/D method within the framework of the in-medium Bethe-Salpeter equation.  Three-momentum restricted three-point functions involving one vector meson and two fermions within a medium of massless fermions are computed within the large-Nc approximation.  By analyzing the chiral asymmetry in the fermionic vacuum, induced by an imbalanced number of fermions and anti-fermions, observed through the nonvanishing condensate of the vector-vector bilinear, we examine the in-medium spectral functions of vector mesons through the dispersion relation.  We discover that the spectrum of vector mesons is significantly influenced by chiral asymmetry in the fermionic vacuum, particularly causing the rho(770) meson to decay into a pair of massless fermions even in the absence of medium effects.

The concept of network scale plays a crucial role in understanding the structure of large-scale networks. This work addresses the challenge of estimating the network scale in a distributed setting, considering potential malicious attacks on some nodes. We focus on the Small-World model, analyzing both the feasibility and efficiency of our proposed estimation algorithm, particularly in scenarios with multiple malicious nodes attacking simultaneously. Our research reveals that, unlike the Byzantine consensus problem, the estimation task can be completed with significantly fewer communication steps and involved nodes, even in the presence of multiple malicious attacks.

In numerical simulations of data for the initial conditions in numerical relativity, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be satisfied. Our proposed method, called the Conformal Transverse-Linear Kernel-based method or CTTK, utilizes the Full Conformal Thorne-Regge Linearized Kernel (FC TLK) framework and incorporates the shift vector as a means to solve the Hamiltonian constraint. Furthermore, the conformal metric is solved by applying the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) to accelerate a $O(N \log N)$ iterative process. Our simulations are accelerated by solving the Poisson equation for the conformal metric with the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). Due to its efficiency, the CTTK handles larger problems more effectively than its predecessors. Consequently, the CTTK supports the solution of higher-dimensional and more physically accurate constraints for gravitational wave initial conditions.

The main experimental issue in the water Cherenkov detector's (JUNO) main challenge stems from its ability to accurately measure the neutrino oscillation parameter $\Delta m^2_{32}$. A critical factor that affects the detector's performance over time is the degradation in electron light yield caused by mass production processes, which in turn could impair the detector's energy resolution stability. To investigate the degradation in the sensitivity of JUNO's photodetectors, we conducted a detailed study on the light detection efficiency and light reflection capabilities of 20-inch PMTs after subjecting them to accelerated aging. As part of this process, the PMTs were subjected to a rapid, high-voltage stress, followed by the collection of Cherenkov radiation from electrons moving at a speed of 0.27c. By analyzing the effects of the accelerated aging on the detector's sensitivity, we found the light detection efficiency decreased by 0.5% to 0.6%, which matches expectations based on the quenching of the PM's photomultiplier tubes. However, the uniform loss of sensitivity across the PM's surface suggests the opportunity for improved performance by adjusting the gain in each cell individually. On the other hand, the water's reflective capabilities remained largely unaffected by the aging process.

In the domain of time series prediction, particularly in complex scenarios with high dimensionality, the data often includes numerous variables that structure an advanced information network. The graph convolutional network (GCN) has emerged as a prominent structural option for GCN-based models. Nonetheless, integrating GCN into GCN-based models introduces difficulties when dealing with high-dimensional data, as it can obscure essential features and obstructions. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative model called the node selection-based graph convolutional network (NS-GCN). This novel approach dynamically chooses the most relevant nodes for GCN in the time series data and constructs a graph-based network structure for each prediction task. By estimating a node selection matrix based on learning, we identify the optimal nodes for GCN and perform prediction accordingly. Our proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to traditional GCN-based models, as showcased by the results on the monthly coal production dataset and the arrow head dataset. By adapting the GCN structure to each series, we optimize its capabilities and overcome the limitations associated with high-dimensional data.

Astronomical observations from the ground are distorted by the Earth's atmosphere, which disperses light and alters its color. To minimize this effect, astronomers use atmospheric dispersion compensators (ADCs) that adjust the dispersion introduced by the atmosphere. To accurately compensate for this distortion, it's essential to understand how the atmosphere affects light differently at various wavelengths. Our team measured the atmospheric dispersion of 40 stars using the Wide Field Camera on the Gran Telescopio CANARIAS and simulated the atmosphere to determine its properties. To describe the atmosphere's properties, we used the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) and compared it to our own derived models, which we found better match our measured data. Our results show that the pressure exponent has minimal impact on atmospheric dispersion but the temperature exponent has a significant effect, particularly at low elevations. We also measured the turbulence structure constant of the atmosphere and observed significant variations during the night, which we suggest periodic temperature changes in the atmosphere are responsible for. Our findings are expected to benefit astronomers in a range of scenarios, such as adaptive optics, spectroscopy, and atmospheric dispersion compensation design.

In the realm of NLP, pre-trained models have become the go-to choice for a wide range of tasks. However, these models often fall short of the desired accuracy levels, which heavily depends on the availability of high-quality labeled data for fine-tuning. Utilizing this abundant yet often underutilized data can be costly and labor-intensive, as it requires the involvement of human experts or pre-trained models to annotate it. Although several approaches have been suggested to mitigate the annotation expenses, they frequently necessitate specialized infrastructure like GPU clusters. This paper introduces a novel method to tackle the dilemma of balancing annotation costs and model performance, without requiring specialized hardware. By leveraging data from multiple human annotators and their respective labels, our approach improves the consistency of models and boosts overall performance, even with limited annotators. We validate our method on datasets for binary, multi-class, and multi-label text classification problems and demonstrate its effectiveness across OpenAI's GPT-2 language model.

Bosonic shadow matter could consist of a vast number of ultralight particles forming a non-condensate ground state with significant local density variations. Its interaction is primarily through gravity, making it a prime candidate for detection through its gravitational effects. Due to its short wavelength, direct detection of this matter is hindered, yet its presence can be indirectly observed through the time- and space-averaged density in its vicinity. We present a method to detect scalar shadow matter by analyzing fluctuations in the density field at scales smaller than its wavelength, utilizing correlation patterns in an optical image. This approach could achieve a detection range of $10^{-15}$ eV to $10^{-9}$ eV for the matter's mass range, making it highly effective within the preferred parameter space.

This paper explores the concept of continuity in basis pursuit (BP) solutions for a non-negative sparse recovery problem on the real line with known sparsity. The BP problem's uniqueness is defined by the property that it yields the same unique answer for any given measurement matrix within an open neighborhood. The study focuses on identifying the conditions under which BP uniqueness occurs at specific sparsity levels and examines how this changes with sparsity. It demonstrates that in some cases, BP uniqueness occurs for all sufficiently large sparsity levels, while in other cases it occurs up to a certain point before disappearing. The study provides examples to illustrate these phenomena. Ultimately, the paper derives lower bounds on reconstruction errors for small BP fail neighborhoods derived from a given fail neighborhood for semideantine rotation matrices.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used solution. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for source code conversion into a format usable on various hardware platforms. Despite options for compiling P4 code, there has been limited exploration of compiling it for the V1Model. We address this gap by developing an innovative compiler backend for the V1Model based on the P4-compatible compiler, demonstrating its effectiveness in both P4-verified and non-parsed programs. Our work contributes to the field by providing enhanced flexibility and performance optimization capabilities for programmers using programmable switches.

In this research, specific methods are proposed to enhance the hybrid high-order method's approximation of the vector transport equation. The study involves a detailed analysis of the low-order Raviart-Thomas space's quadrilateral/rectangular basis, ultimately enabling the formulation of the transported field within this element. The resulting enhancements preserve the superior convergence rates of the HHM while resolving the vector transport equation accurately; the newly formulated weak problem demonstrates optimal convergence rates in both $L^2$ and $H(\textrm{div})$ norms. The effectiveness of these proposals is assessed through four established tests - continuity, compressibility, and an enhanced version of the "checkerboard" test - as well as a continuous quality test, with outstanding results demonstrated in all cases.

Emerging technology, federated learning, presents a promising approach for creating equitable machine learning models without compromising sensitive data.  To address the potential biases in federated models, a novel framework integrates fairness constraints within each client's local training process.  This framework combines multiple methods.  First, it enforces specific fairness metrics at the client level.  Second, it applies different privacy techniques, including FedAvg and FedClip, to limit information leakage during federated training.  Our studies demonstrate the capabilities of this framework in achieving balanced federated models that safeguard user privacy.  Notably, we observe that incorporating privacy techniques has a greater impact on utility and fairness than enforcing fairness metrics.  Conversely, fairness metrics show varying outcomes across different models and datasets.

Using the LHCb experiment's data, a new analysis has examined the difference between $K$ mesons and other particles against various $B_c$ states. This search targets the $3^-$ excited state of $B_c^+$, denoted as $3^-{(1,2)}$, in a decay process of $J/\psi$ and $D_s^+$. Initial results revealed no difference from the expected outcome, with the $K^+$ maximum false positive rate at 0.26 picometers and the $K^+$ false difference not surpassing 1.3 picometers nor below -13 picometers. This lack of observed signal does not rule out the $2D$ state, with the $K^+$ maximum false positive rate at 0.22 picometers and the $K^+$ false difference not surpassing 1.4 picometers nor below -12 picometers.

A new class of estimators, known as continuous-stage Runge-Kutta estimates, is proposed to approximate solution trajectories of initial value problems for ordinary differential equations. This method yields a higher degree of accuracy, specifically an additional order of precision, compared to traditional Runge-Kutta methods. The efficiency of these estimators is first evaluated, and the resulting classes of optimally estimators are identified for specific scenarios, including general multistage methods with fixed and adaptive step sizes.

Recent breakthroughs in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have led to a surge in their applications across various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. The scalability of GPU clusters for training large-scale DNNs has been a major challenge. Data-parallel learning, which divides training data across multiple GPUs, is a widely used approach to overcome this challenge. Although this strategy works well for smaller models, it runs into limitations when the model size equals or exceeds the total number of trainable parameters. For these scenarios, a model-parallel approach is needed. In this paper, regional critic training (RCT) is introduced as a novel method to scale DNNs beyond the limits of data-parallel learning. By partitioning DNNs into data-parallel groups, each with a unique copy of the network and data subset, RCT communicates weights gradient-wise to synchronize the models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RCT on four popular training scenarios, including data-parallel baseline, tensor-parallel, all-reduce, and hierarchical data parallelism, showing significant speed improvements over existing solutions.

Despite significantly simpler dynamics in two-dimensional systems, three-dimensional (3D) chaotic scattering exhibits more intricate and diverse behavior. A key discovery in our study of the 3D weak dissipation problem is that it exhibits Wada basins, which were not a characteristic feature in three 2D problems related to it. These Wada basins, which are found in all three attractors, have a complex fractal structure. Furthermore, our research indicates that there are actually multiple attractors resulting from the system undergoing temporary chaotic transients. The presence of these Wada basins, however, does not seem to be linked to specific topological properties but rather to intricate interactions among the basins.

A top-quark decay pattern is explored where the produced particles, top quarks and light scalars, are not generated directly coupled. Instead, the coupling of these particles to the Higgs boson results in an indirect interaction, producing a distinct and experimentally feasible production method for the light scalars at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Though indirectly created, the produced light scalars have a relatively long lifespan and can be detected by leaving signs of their interaction along a detectable path in experiments. We examine the feasibility of this process by analyzing various theoretical models for the coupling of these particles, considering their potential detection at the LHC across a broad range of parameter space. Additionally, we extend our analysis to other possible decay patterns of the light scalars, considering their potential detection as a product of top-quark decay.

This study introduces the first reference dataset, AQAI, comprising 102 videos with diverse backgrounds and orientations, depicting everyday actions like walking, eating, driving, etc. Furthermore, this work outlines a novel attention-guided model that extracts spatial and temporal features from videos in distinct frames. The extracted features are then analyzed using a hierarchical attention module to capture the most informative regions within the temporal frames. The model's training and evaluation were conducted on the AQAI dataset. Additionally, extensive experiments were carried out under different settings to evaluate its performance on activity recognition in videos.

This research explores the thermodynamic properties and feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis in RN-AdS black holes influenced by a scalar field. We analyzed how the horizon areas of outer and inner black holes respond to changes in various parameters. Consequently, we determined the conditions necessary to avoid a naked singularity. Furthermore, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of the system using the first law of thermodynamics and verified its thermal stability through eigenvalue analysis of the specific heat.

The phenomenon of starlight has been the source of numerous myths and legends since ancient times. Contrary to popular belief, scientists have only have a limited understanding of how stars are formed. This book will provide a comprehensive and accessible explanation of the scientific knowledge regarding the lifecycle of stars, from the initial stages of star inception to the diverse types of stars and the ultimate destinations of stars when they cease to shine.

The Joint Historical Entropy (JHE) serves as a metric to gauge how much data contributes to understanding past joint distributions. In this paper, we explore how to compute the JHE of M samples of size N using the Nested Sampling method, an algorithm for approximate Bayesian computation. We show that JHE can be estimated more efficiently by focusing on the most unlikely data values. To demonstrate, we apply our approach to calculating the entropy of M particles in 1D and 3D settings, as well as estimating the entropy of the size of the largest cluster in N samples of n independent Bernoulli trials with probability p.

We establish that the convolution of a Dirac measure with an initial data for a nonlinear conservation law results in a measure-valued solution. This is to be expected since the operation is associative. The law $u_t + f(u)_x = 0$ involves a entropy solution $u$ with values in $\mathbb R$. It has been observed by Bressan and Goatin that initial data consisting of measures can also generate measure-valued solutions. A specific subcase of this operation, when applied to functions and Dirac measures, yields a measure-valued solution which, for a given function $u_0$, remains the same as the Cauchy problem with $u_0$. This result holds under the understanding that it mainly addresses the interaction between waves. We demonstrate this by examining the effect of noise on solution behaviors. This operation can be seen to reveal effects of wave interactions.

The proliferation of IoT devices has accelerated innovation and advancement, yet its rapid expansion poses significant security risks due to vulnerabilities in the devices. A critical challenge arises from the fact that security tools on resource-constrained devices, such as microcontrollers, often lack the computational power to process large datasets, rendering them ineffective. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach codeless network intrusion detection is introduced, allowing the analysis of entire packet contents while reducing computational demands and enhancing accuracy. By applying this technique, the entire communication between two devices can be reconstructed, facilitating the analysis of complete context and enabling the labeling of entire sessions as normal or malicious. By leveraging this approach, a hybrid model combining Bayesian statistics and coding theory, referred to as NBcoded, is developed to classify entire sessions, and this is evaluated using datasets representing microcontroller-based communications where malicious activities include DDoS and data theft. The results show that the NBcoded approach yields superior accuracy, particularly against DDoS attacks with 99.51% accuracy, and the source code for this approach is available at https://github.com/lorenzo-bottalico/NBcoded.

This research aims to establish specific bounds for solvable groups. We found optimal or near-optimal growth limits for abelian-by-cyclic groups across all scales, as well as found for symmetric groups. We found optimal growth limits for halved cyclic groups. We also determined a range for the growth of metacyclic groups, which we showed to be capable of having up to multiple distinct bounds. We found that in terms of growth, the "ends" of metacyclic groups can take on a full range of possible values. We also found similar but less precise but still significant results for the growth limits of Fitting groups.

Epidemiologists seek effective and efficient ways to gauge the flow of people in public spaces to assess the spread of biological agents. To achieve this, they require accurate data on the movement of individuals in these spaces. To facilitate this process, we have developed a computational system that uses cameras to track the movement of people in these spaces. By utilizing computer vision and machine learning techniques, our system can automatically detect and monitor the movement of people without the need for special equipment such as sensors or RFID tags. To further improve the system's accuracy, we have developed a novel method for handling real-time data streams, allowing us to predict the movement of individuals in real-time. Our solution has been successfully tested in a study of the spread of infectious diseases, yielding valuable insights into the movement of people in public spaces.

Optimizing power grid operations is crucial for reducing costs and maintaining stability.
Linear programming problems are effectively solved using the quantum linear systems algorithm, which has exponential advantages.
In this study, we show how to apply this to the DC-Optimal Power Flow (DC-OPF) method and obtain solutions close to those from traditional solvers with potential for substantial reductions in computational time.
Our approach yields solutions that are at most four times larger than those from conventional solvers, demonstrating the potential for substantial gains.
We explore various factors influencing the accuracy of our quantum solution and discuss its implications.

In recent years, significant advancements in machine learning have led to the development of methods that enable the automatic detection of patterns and fundamental laws within complex datasets. This research examines how these machine learning techniques can be utilized to identify physical principles and the behavior of systems, often resulting in discrepancies that reveal inconsistencies in existing models. A key challenge lies in establishing a solid theoretical framework for machine learning models derived from theoretical physics, thereby enhancing the reliability of these methods in real-world applications.

This study investigates the presence of heavy particles for the mass range of 100 to 5000 GeV that stability is characterized by a long lifespan, by utilizing a novel search methodology that utilizes muon detectors and another based on tracking systems and a detector called a calorimeter, by applying it to data collected by the ATLAS detector, by using proton-proton collisions at a energy of 13 TeV, by using a total dataset of data of 100 billion events. The search methodology using muon detectors targets particles that emit large amounts of secondary particles and another based on tracking systems and a detector called a calorimeter that is sensitive to particles moving in pairs with low energy and another that is focused on particles moving in a particular direction and another that is sensitive to particles moving in another particular direction. The search methodology using muon detectors found no significant signals above the standard model predictions in datasets collected between April 2015 and June 2018. The search methodology using muon detectors set limits on the cross-section of particles for various scenarios of long-lived particles for long-lived particles having lifetimes greater than 0.1 nanoseconds and another for long-lived particles having lifetimes less than 0.1 nanoseconds. The search methodology using muon detectors found no significant signals above the standard model predictions in datasets collected between April 2015 and June 2018.
