In federated learning, client participation during training often suffers from bottlenecks imposed by asynchronous aggregation, which has led researchers to limit client participation in order to ease the burden on the server. To address this limitation, our work examines the effect of allowing unrestricted client gradients in the case of asynchronous federated averaging. By exploring the relationship between aggregation delays and historical client gradients, our theoretical analysis proves that a averaging list can be maintained such that the averaged model converges to an $\epsilon$-stationary point in a specific time frame. This list incorporates older gradients but ensures that its size remains logarithmically bounded. Furthermore, by incorporating the inflation property, our list can function as a variant of Optimistic Federated Averaging, delivering improved convergence performance. Experimentally, Delib, a distributed library based on TCP without any additional message protocols or data structures, verifies our findings by pragmatically implementing our averaging list and showcasing its efficacy in real-world applications.

This study delves into a space of non-linear functionals, specifically within a Banach algebra of functions that are polynomial and tempered, alongside an analysis of how differential operators function as continuous endomorphisms from this space to itself.

The quantum swampland criteria imply that the fractional amount of dark matter, denoted as Omega_d, must be less than a specified threshold which is directly related to the dark matter's largest cluster scale, specifically, a maximum value of scale (x_max) should be less than approximately 10 to the power of 11. This means that the largest clusters can only contain a minimal fraction (x_max) of dark matter. This condition is particularly significant for dark matter candidates that are candidates for forming supermassive black holes in the early universe. In this paper, the author examines x for supermassimal black holes over a broad range of masses and finds minimal values of approximately 1 to 10 to the power of 4 for masses ranging from about 10 to the power of 16 grams to 10 to the power 24 grams. The author proposes that a fraction of dark matter consists of primordial black holes with masses around 1 to 10 to the power of 21 grams, which are a potential source of gamma-ray background observed from the sky.

Biological membranes are primarily composed of lipid bilayers, whose properties can be significantly influenced by the incorporation of transmembrane proteins. The restricted movement of this proteins, often referred to as 'trapping,' has been revealed to yield richer and more intricate bilayer behavior when modeled at the level of coarse-grained detail. In our investigation, we employed a simplified, yet realistic, model of a bilayer containing fixed transmembrane proteins to replicate specific features observed in real-world scenarios, such as the spacing and orientation patterns, as well as the formation of voids and structures resembling gaps. In addition, our study further explores the emergence of undulating surface patterns in scenarios involving more dynamic, floating proteins, whose behavior we attributed to the interplay of entropic forces arising from the confinement of out-of-plane bilayer deviations.

The effectiveness of specific ternary nitrides such as ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2 as effective lattice matches for GaN is examined for the first time. Two successful methods of growing GaN on these matches via molecular beam epitaxy are achieved, via specific templates of GaN/GaP and GaN/SiC. Results reveal strong in-plane compressive strain upon bonding to ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2, countering the natural expansion when bonding to SiC or the underlying Si. The observed strain induces an orthorhombic distortion within the GaN crystal, yielding a substantial increase in electron hole hole conductivity while retaining a direct band at the bonding to SiC and underlying Si. Results reveal significant enhancement in mobility values at high temperatures at 80K GaN on the two matches closely mirror ZnO. Results reveal strong enhancement in mobility values at high temperatures at 80K GaN on the two matches to ZnO. Results reveal strong enhancement in mobility values at high temperatures at 80K GaN on the two matches to ZnO.

Several advanced path planning techniques rely on knowledge representation that creates a detailed but complex model of the environment, resulting in high computational costs. To reduce this high cost and make these algorithms more practical to implement on marine robots, our research presents a straightforward Gaussian process-based method for learning a sparse time-difference learning rule. This approach leverages temporal transfer to learn a value function that prioritizes the most critical features, yielding lower computation costs. We incorporate the Bayesian framework to automatically manage the algorithm's parameters, preventing over-fitting. We integrate the parameters of the Gaussian process into the temporal difference learning framework using variational inference for scalable computations. We incorporate the derived sparse temporal difference learning rule into the bootstrap kernel-temporal difference algorithm to develop an approximate temporal difference estimator. We incorporate this simplified estimator into multiple policy and value iteration algorithms to develop low-cost learning methods. We thoroughly review the proposed approach and compare its performance with other commonly used TD algorithms through theoretical analysis. We demonstrate the practical feasibility of this approach by conducting a series of simulation experiments in an underwater robotic system. We investigate the impact of various factors, such as spatial complexity, sampling rates, and exploration strategies, on computing costs. We analyze the trade-offs between these costs and the accuracy of the learned policies. We assess the effectiveness of our learned policies by comparing them with optimal strategies derived from classic planning algorithms.

We examine isothermic surfaces with complex conjugate eigenvectors on the real axis, focusing on how Darboux and Calapso transformations interact within this context. We show that both transformations preserve surfaces with this property and have real representations that maintain the property of being isothermic and meromorphic surface, specifically in the case of isometric conditions.

We introduce and analyze a nonparametric estimator, known as the conditional expectation operator, which takes a conditional distribution as its input and produces an operator as output, based on a given input random vector with support in a bounded subset of R^d. This approach generalizes various forms of conditional mappings, such as regression functions and transformation operators, and is applicable to scenarios involving operators on given subspaces of L_1 R^d or L_∞ R^d. We demonstrate the consistency of this estimator and provide a nonasymptotic risk bound for its performance when measured in the L_∞ norm. This risk bound remains finite even in low-dimensional settings and remains robust across L_∞ norms on given subspaces of L_1 R^d or L_∞ R^d. Furthermore, we develop a new conditional density estimator based on this framework, which remains meaningful even when the conditional density does not exist. We obtain nonasymptotic upper bounds for the risk of this estimator, measured in terms of the L_∞ norm over given subspaces of L_1 R^d or L_∞ R^d, and show that this risk bound is independent of the dimensionality of the given subspaces. This result leads to a novel approach for the nonparametric estimation of conditional distributions, and we establish both convergence rates and the minimax risk for this estimation problem.

This study introduces $\lambda$-analogues of the r-Stirling numbers of the secondary kind, with $S_\lambda\left\{\begin{matrix}n\\m\\r\end{matrix}\right\}$ denoting this concept. The paper defines and examines the properties of these $\lambda$-analogues and presents $\lambda$-similarities for r-Stirling numbers of the secondary kind and its variants: cycle index sum and $\lambda$-analogues of cycle index sum. Additionally, the paper identifies and explains the relationships between r-Stirling numbers of the secondary kind, its variant: cycle index sum, and its further analogue: $\lambda$-analogues of cycle index sum.

The不断扩大的临时知识图谱正变得越来越重要. 多个重要任务, 如实体检索, 实体完成和文本引导的实体完成等, 都依赖于知识图谱的链接预测. 然而传统的临时知识图谱表示学习模型由于存储完整的子结构而面临巨大的计算负担. 为了解决这个问题, 我们提出了一种基于静态模型的方法, 通过预测每个时间步长的关系来预测链接, 从而大大减少了内存占用. 实验结果显示, 我们的模型不仅在预测链接方面的性能与完整的模型相当,而且还显著提高了训练和推理的效率.

We investigate the robust equivalence of shift dynamical systems and corresponding graph C*-algebras. Our study demonstrates that a fundamental criterion for robust equivalence, initially formulated in terms of dynamical systems, coincides with a graph-theoretic formulation. Additionally, we derive a significant consequence: a graph with finite out-degrees is robustly equivalent to the Floyd graph if and only if it possesses a finite resolution.

In a hot QCD medium with a strong magnetic field, the thermal decay properties of heavy mesons consisting of strange and charm quarks are analyzed. The transport coefficients of the process, including the dissipation rate and momentum degradation in the presence of a magnetic field, are calculated. The influence of the magnetic field and anisotropy on the dissipation properties of the heavy mesons is examined in detail. The resulting decay widths of these mesons are found to have both real and imaginary components, thus giving rise to the phenomenon of oscillating decay and potentially, decay delay in the presence of a magnetic field.

Although pre-trained language models like BERT have greatly improved question-answering systems, they still rely heavily on manual feature engineering and fail to utilize knowledge graphs (KGs) effectively. To address these limitations, we introduce a model that integrates label propagation, allowing it to utilize structured knowledge within KGs and combine this with learned language representations from BERT. By applying this model to two datasets and two KGs, we demonstrate its ability to outperform existing baselines, showcasing the benefits of integrating structured knowledge with language models for enhanced question-answering performance.

This dimension elevation technique, known as 'folding', combines two lower-dimensional linear error-correcting codes to create a new code in higher dimensions with similar properties. It has been utilized to create the first known extendable codes in dimensions beyond three. We apply this folding property to specific low-dimensional codes, including Hadamard codes and new binary codes with high rates and dimensions, to produce enhanced codes in higher dimensions. These enhanced codes exhibit improved relative distances and rates while maintaining extendability.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential of a novel technique known as in-context learning, which leverages carefully selected examples to enhance performance on unfamiliar tasks without the need for explicit instruction or modification of the model itself. A prominent study has highlighted the significance of strategic example selection in improving performance; however, the choice of examples is hindered by the vast number of possible choices and the limited understanding of their effects. To address these challenges, we have undertaken a comprehensive evaluation of different prompt engineering methods, focusing on the influence of various training examples and the inclusion of multiple choice options from unexplored domains.
The paper is a detailed documentation of the specific paper "The Krumm-Lin's $\mathscr{L}$-invariant".

We have developed a Rydberg atom-based Rydberg spectroscopy technique that leverages multifrequency microwave (MW) radiation. The novel technique's data analysis has been enhanced by integrating a deep learning approach, which has enabled superior performance in microwave frequency retrieval. Specifically, our enhanced binary classification neural network achieved an astounding 9 rydberg atom accuracy and has been validated through rigorous testing under rigorous noise conditions. The training data for this innovation was generated through a cutting-edge simulation based on the time-dependent Thomas-Angerman model. The efficacy of our binary neural network training has been thoroughly documented in this paper.

UGC 8839, a nearby spiral galaxy, exhibits an unusually large and symmetrical disk despite having very little star formation activity. A study utilizing a high-resolution spectroscopic observation reveals significant details about the galaxy's dynamics, showing that the inner parts exhibit Hubble flow while the outer parts show a slower rotation rate. Analysis indicates the presence of a massive invisible component, accounting for about 4.3e11 Msun, within the galaxy's disk, while the halo's total mass is estimated to be only about ten times the mass of the disk, contradicting typical findings for dark matter halos. Additionally, the comparison of dynamical mass estimates with mass estimates derived from stellar light suggests that the disk's stars account for a minor portion of the total mass. Furthermore, the magnitude of the mass estimates differs from the mass derived from the galaxy's stellar velocity dispersion by a factor of about three, suggesting the presence of old stars with substantial orbital movements in addition to the measured systemic movement.

This dissertation investigates various measures of complexity within the study of quaseregular mappings. Initially, it establishes the correct definition and properties of Hausdorff dimension for these mappings, correcting a previously erroneous definition by P\"{o}hltz. Subsequent research focuses on determining whether certain topological properties, such as the Hausdorff dimension or separability, of the Julia set in quasiregular mappings correspond to those of the underlying space. Employing techniques like Riemann surface composition and Kelvin's inversion, the dissertation provides examples demonstrating that the Hausdorff dimension and separability of the Julia set can differ from the values defined by the underlying space's dimension. Nevertheless, under the condition where a quasiregular mapping's degree equals one, the underlying space's separability is reflected in the Julia set's separability. To expand our understanding of the dynamics within quasiregular mappings, the dissertation also examines the density and distribution of periodic points in these mappings. Utilising the dimension of the Julia set and applying methods from quasiconformal theory, the dissertation presents conditions under which the set of non-recurring wandering points occupies either negligible measure or constitutes a substantial portion of the phase space. Additionally, the dissertation considers the set of non-recurrent points associated with quasiregular version of the Holomorphic Shilov boundary theorem.

Our investigation into Mars' gravity waves utilized data from MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN satelites to understand their global distribution, frequency range, and vertical propagation. The resulting map revealed that gravity waves are ubiquitous on both hemispheres of Mars, with higher occurrence and intensity in the northern hemisphere during its winter season. These waves are primarily found within the 1-4 millihertz frequency band and generally propagate up to 130 km in altitude, with notable exceptions reaching as high as 175 km. Moreover, our research indicated that gravity waves are more likely to reach the upper thermosphere in the winter hemisphere, where their activity is also more pronounced. Interestingly, our analysis also uncovered that gravity waves are more likely to persist during winter in the northern hemisphere and spring and fall seasons in the southern hemisphere, with their higher activity during the southern winter. What's more, our research showed that while solar radiation influences gravity waves in the summer hemisphere, their behavior is less受制于 solar radiation in the winter hemisphere, possibly due to their higher base level during this season. To sum up, our study has generated a groundbreaking global map of gravity waves in the Martian thermosphere, where their frequency range and propagation distance have been precisely measured and found to vary seasonally and hemispherically.

The LHC has demonstrated its capability for generating enormous collision energies, achieving record-breaking momentum transfers in head-on particle collisions.  Physicists anticipate that lepton pairs will be created through quantum interactions between motional charges.  This study examines data from 2013, 2015, and 2016 ALICE lead-lead ultra-peripheral collision experiments.  Researchers used J/ψ leptons to explore the electric field's impact on a barrier-free system.  Findings indicate that momentum transfer occurs within a 2.8 to 3.5 femtometer range, consistent with expectations based on previous experiments.  This study provides new insights into the quantum interaction between nuclei with high nuclear charges and massive ions.  Leptons produced in this process offer a valuable tool for probing and mapping the complex relationship between space and time in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions.  This work has been published in Phys. Rev. Lett. 30, 2017 and the collaboration involved an extensive group of scientists from 2013 to 2016 experiments.

Current research in sound design focuses on learning sound creation techniques
using neural networks, but these models often lack control and predictability
when applied to sound creation based on visual cues. To overcome these limitations,
we developed SoundBank, a comprehensive sound library with over 14 thousand unique
sounds and introduced the various acoustic properties sound objects possess.
Furthermore, we developed a method to manually create sounds that align with these
acoustic properties, enabling better understanding and control over the sound
creation process. Next, we trained a neural network to predict sound parameters
based on images and the desired acoustic properties, which we then used to generate
sounds. Our approach surpasses that of previous unsupervised sound generation models,
and in our tests, sound generators based on visual cues produced more consistent
and predictable sounds. We also introduced the first sound design task specifically
tailored for the SoundBank dataset, and found that our sound generator can be used
in sound design tasks, and even combined with human input to enhance its output.

Recurrent Neural Networks have garnered significant interest for their capability to model sequential data representations. However, their application to machine learning tasks in temporal contexts has been relatively underexplored. This research delves into the advantages and limitations of using Recurrent Neural Networks for temporal data processing. It compares and contrasts various recurrent architectures and assessments methods to determine their efficacy, specifically investigating: (1) the transformative potential of Recurrent Neural Networks for temporal data; (2) the sequential nature of temporal data; and (3) the significance of sliding windows in recurrent recurrent neural networks. We evaluate the recurrent models and non-recurrent baselines across five diverse datasets from different applications and report the results of our findings.

To determine the ideal pandemic management approach, we must minimize losses in both lives and income, with the optimal strategy being the earliest possible implementation of strict measures, followed by a gradual relaxation until the epidemic subsides, with a rapid recovery ensuing. This conclusion holds under a broad array of conditions, transcending specific societal and medical contexts. In light of this finding, individual, bi-national, and international cooperation is essential to ensure swift and uniform adoption of strict measures worldwide.

The data science community has recently concentrated on the concept of model interpretability to clarify the choices made by machine learning algorithms. What's missing is an examination of interpretability for the input data itself. Our proposed 'data interpretability' approach utilizes Shapley values over a comprehensive machine learning pipeline, allowing users to understand how individual data points and subsets influence model predictions and model features in turn. Our data cleaning tool then allows for the identification of data issues based on this new approach, and successfully handles datasets with over 100,000 data points and 200 potential features.

This text highlights how modern enumerative geometry draws upon statistics, combinatorics, and topology to address unresolved queries. By presenting itself as a narrative of interaction, it aims to inspire researchers in both domains.

High magnetic ordering temperatures in Mn$_3$Sn triangular antiferromagnets allow the switch of an anomalous Hall effect at the megapascal pressure scale, which can be manipulated within a feasible pressure range. An helium droplet counter demonstrates that the Hall mobility in Mn$_3$Sn is up to 10,000 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ at room temperature, highlighting its potential as a multifunctional device.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the HPC and Scientific community's adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNN) and offers an overview of Dingbat, a service designed to facilitate exploration of potential DNNs in High-Performance Computing. DNNs have shown remarkable success in recent years, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in various high-precision classification and regression challenges. Its universal approximation capability makes it applicable to a wide range of problems, including tasks previously handled by regression models like Support Vector Regression and Kernel Ridge Regression. However, training DNNs poses significant challenges due to the massive number of parameters involved, often necessitating substantial computational resources and sometimes even supercomputing power for feasible training times.

This paper delves into a specific eigenvalue problem involving a steklov-type term, a robin-type term, and the gradient of functions. We demonstrate that under certain conditions on the boundary, this problem possesses infinitely many finite-dimensional eigenspaces. Additionally, when considering the special case where the robin term is absent, we show that the problem is capable of having infinite-dimensional eigenspaces.

Hypergraph reconstruction through the analysis of data is known as the reverse HPP. This process has garnered more attention recently since it's applicable to various fields like quantizing systems, performing dimension reduction, and understanding topological features. We introduce a new method using the non-backtracking and the oriented non-backtracking matrix to HPP. The proposed method harnesses the non-zero eigenvalues of these matrices. We developed a criterion based on these eigenvalues and formulated a systematic approach to determine the edge weights in the hypergraph. With the aid of C++ and Matlab implementations, we tested our method on synthetic datasets, showing its effectiveness in reconstructing the given hypergraphs accurately. We developed two implementations: the first uses selected eigenvalues, while the second employs all eigenvalues. We discovered that the primary factor influencing our algorithm is the choice of a parameter 'R', which represents the minimum degree of the hypergraph. We tested our algorithm on real-world datasets including Kaggle and PyTorch examples and discovered that using the all eigenvalues version consistently produced superior results. Notably, the parameter R can be set automatically without compromising the performance. We achieved a F1-score of 0.91 on the Kaggle dataset 'Real World from 3D' and '0.81 Points on the line'.

In medical image report annotation tasks like COVID detection, accurate findings are hindered by ambiguous and redundant information in clinical X-ray images. Current approaches rely on noisy, manually collected annotations which are time-consuming and limited in scope. This research suggests that radiological reports correspond more accurately to 2D CT images than to actual X-ray images. A new dataset is introduced with high-quality annotations derived from CT scans of 14,000 patients, and a novel loss function is proposed to bridge the gap between handwritten and automated X-ray annotations. This new data and loss function enhance X-ray data efficiently without necessitating additional patient imaging, and experimental results demonstrate its efficacy in report learning tasks, outperforming existing methods in four tested scenarios.

M. LeBrun and J. Marmura discovered a non-existence result for contact structures on certain over- and nearly-Stein contact structures in 2006. 
Our work provides a wider class of manifolds and surfaces that meet these requirements, incorporating Euler characteristics and Thurston norms. 
Additionally, we prove an extended version of the result, with specific conditions on Euler characteristics and Thurston norms of surfaces related to their Euler characteristics and norms. 
Furthermore, we find specific examples of contact structures on a manifold where every representing surface fails to satisfy specific criteria and we explore surface-related questions with an emphasis on M. Marcut's work from 2015.

The low entropy emission characteristic of microcavity lasers stems from its narrow, unidirectional output, which sets it apart from conventional lasers in terms of entropy generation and photon dispersal. This phenomenon is rarely examined due to the elusive nature of entropy in physical systems. However, leveraging microcavity lasers'stray tails" observed in experimental setup images enables the calculation of entropy generation and quantifies their unidirectional emission. Our findings reveal that the entropy generation rate during lasing is significantly higher during the build-up phase compared to the steady state, as entropy generation rate is directly proportional to the difference in stimulated and total emission intensities. Moreover, the entropy produced per photon during the build-up phase is several orders of magnitude greater than in the steady state, making it an optimal choice for entropically assessing microcavity lasers's unidirectional emission.

The primary function of exchange tokens in decentralized finance is to facilitate transactions. Due to their inherent volatility, however, exchange tokens may fail to serve this purpose effectively, leading users to seek alternative methods for hedging against price fluctuations. This study aims to address the issue by examining the relative value stability of major exchange tokens compared to traditional currencies and to explore the potential reasons behind this instability. Specifically, the relative value of these tokens is evaluated using the widely accepted mean absolute deviation from parity method. Results reveal that exchange tokens are relatively more valuable than traditional currencies, with Bitcoin showing the greatest value appreciation. This findings attribute the token's increased value to its scarcity. This investigation offers a novel perspective on the stability of exchange tokens within its current context, shedding new light on their potential as a medium of exchange and as a store of value.

We verify an open hypothesis from Catterall et al. (2017) that allows solving the generalized Kardar-Parisi-Zark equation exactly for any set of finite noise realizations in one and two spatial dimensions. Our solution methodology involves the use of the inverse scattering technique for the Zakharov-Shabat system.

Our analysis of MMS spacecraft potential data revealed compressive turbulence at sub-ion scales within the solar wind, characterized by a break occurring between 5 and 10 ion scales of 1 kHz. The turbulence was characterized by random fluctuating frequencies within the 1-10 kHz range, resulting in significant dissipation within the 1-10 kHz frequency band, consistent with the expected D/4π rate. The turbulent variations primarily affected electron and ion temperatures, leading to pronounced heating of electrons over ions.

Synchronized acceleration of electrons within an accelerator is crucial for the efficiency of next-generation X-ray Free-Electron Lasers, particularly for producing extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray pulses. We demonstrate that the modification of the chirp-taper technique allows for the generation of attosecond XUV and soft X-ray pulses by combining it with the study of the underlying electron dynamics and their impact on bunching. This research reveals that by the point where the synchronization of the accelerator and the laser synchronization match, the electron's rotating motion reaches its maximum, producing powerful attosecond pulses. We have used numerical modeling to predict that this scheme can yield the generation of a 40-as pulse at 13.5-eV using specific accelerator and synchronization parameters, as well as a 200-eV, 36-as pulse at 7.5-eV under different conditions. This new scheme has the potential to produce very short, highly energetic pulses in the soft X-ray range.

The growth of turbulent fluctuations in a stratified flow under specific conditions is estimated using models based on linear inertial turbulence theories. These models assume that the turbulence originates from the interaction between two opposing shear turbulence sources, with the turbulence intensity and temperature variations decaying exponentially from these sources. To calculate turbulence properties, the models utilize inertial dissipation rates and finite-time temperature and velocity difference probability density functions. These models effectively describe and predict turbulent behavior in laboratory and atmospheric environments due to their high level of overlap between temperature and velocity PDAs. Ultimately, the accuracy of these models in determining PDDs is evaluated by comparing with direct numerical simulations and observing significant deviations at higher p values.

Election manipulation through dividing electorates into regions is a centuries-old issue. 
The combination of inefficient region-based voting systems and deliberate influence 
by politicians amplifies the impact, resulting in numerous contested elections. 
Partisan biases in such cases depend on the manner in which electorates are shaped 
and divided, an process referred to as influence in this context. 
The aim of this study is to introduce a method for measuring influence through 
assigning voters to regions using an approach inspired by statistical physics, 
a method known as the marked Ising model through simulated cooling. 
We implement this method for general regions and also specifically for districts 
defined by their boundaries, taking into account the concept of influence and 
especially minimizing the lengths of districts' outlines in our algorithm. 
The proposed method has and will be used in collaboration with relevant parties 
for the redesign of Europe's election regions, particularly those in Belgium and 
Croatia, to eliminate evident manipulations and achieve a fairer electoral system. 
The algorithm successfully minimizes the lengths of regions' outlines while also 
producing a wide range of customizable outcomes that allow for controlling the 
level of partisan biases in Europe, specifically Belgium and Croatia, and 
enabling a thorough analysis and evaluation of the effectiveness of this method.

This paper focuses on developing an efficient image processing technique to accurately identify and distinguish various types of defects in patterned fabric images. A novel feature set is introduced, combining the Gabor and Hough transforms, to effectively represent fabric patterns and facilitate the detection of defects. This is complemented by a low-rank decomposition method that removes noise and ensures the targeted focus on fabric patterns. Through experimental analysis, it is demonstrated that this proposed technique outperforms existing methods in achieving a high accuracy rate of defect recognition.

In recent years, deep learning has made significant advancements in automated visual guidance systems. However, most policy optimization algorithms struggle to effectively adapt these models in real-world settings. Reinforcement learning policy optimization techniques often rely on a predefined policy model, leading to the overfitting of the training distribution and poor generalization abilities. Additionally, these algorithms face challenges in balancing the degree of exploration during training, resulting in inefficient policy optimization. To address these issues, we incorporate an I/O minimization regularizer into the reinforcement learning policy optimization process to enhance the generalization capabilities of the policy model. Experimental evaluations on the MuJoCo simulation and complex visual tasks reveal significant improvements, yielding up to a 50% improvement, compared to traditional policy optimization methods.

As a black hole gains mass, its increase slows, leading to an asymptotic limit on its mass, despite initially losing mass at a faster rate. This phenomenon suggests that the standard formula for calculating mass gain from radiation and particle emission may need adjustment at higher quantum gravity levels, or that alternative mass loss mechanisms could be further limited by the universe's expansion.

The earliest stars that formed within the universe's history may have included massive Pop III binaries capable of producing detectable gravitational waves (GWs) through interactions within a host galaxy's central bulge. To estimate GW generation rates, researchers created two Boltzmann equation models that simulate the evolution of Pop III binaries until they spiral into each other due to gravitational radiation. One model assumes the binaries remain intact, while the other considers the likelihood of primordial three-body interactions disrupting them. Results indicate GW generation rates depend heavily on stellar collision parameters to the power of -5.5 to -6.5, with lower values resulting from theoretical discrepancies. Rates found for stable binaries range from approximately 1000 to 50000 per cubic parsec. However, for Pop III stars bound within nuclear star clusters, primordial disruption through primordial collapse produces a more realistic distribution of binary fractions and shorter formation timescales than the fragmentation process. This leads to substantial reductions in the minimum and median binary separation distributions from 1000 AU to 0.1-10 AU for stable binaries with initial orbital periods of a few hundred years. Rates of GW emission from Pop III remnants within these nuclear star clusters could potentially exceed 1000 per cubic parsec for binaries with masses exceeding thirty solar masses. Despite the inherent theoretical uncertainties, existing GW detectors could potentially detect GWs emitted by Pop III remnants in the bulges of nearby galaxies. Power distribution operators rely on incident detection systems to identify and locate faults in high-voltage distribution feeders. This data enables operators to initiate the appropriate response for system restoration. In this paper, incident detection methods that leverage voltage and current measurements from a feeder's substation and substations are evaluated. Our analysis encompasses incident detection techniques that rely on phorators, reclosers, and advanced algorithmic approaches leveraging power flow models and machine learning algorithms. The findings highlight the operational benefits and challenges of each method in terms of implementation feasibility and performance effectiveness.

Our study focuses on the decay process of the $X(3872)$, a charmonium-like state, as it breaks down into a $J/\psi$ and a pion, along with other potential particles, in an attempt to shed light on its unknown internal composition. We utilize the Flatt\'{e} formula to formulate the interaction between the $D^0\bar D^{*0}$ and $D^*S$ systems, solving the dispersion relation to derive the wave function. Through further analysis of our model's results, we offer insights into the nature of the $X(3872)$ state, particularly with regard to its broad $\eta'D J/\psi$ decay process.

We define specific categories associated with quadratic forms over fields, establishing relationships between these categories and identifying invariants of the quadratic forms based on category morphisms. It is decided which quadratic forms have a non-trivial endomorphism ring, and the minimal invariant identified. Furthermore, for the purpose of comparison, we developed categories over symmetric bilinear forms and identified their relationship with the quadratic form categories, confirming that they yield the same category. Consequently, we concluded that any characteristic of a quadratic form over a field of characteristic 2 is also a characteristic of any quadratic form over its quadratic closure.

Text-based games provide a highly scalable environment for natural language models to learn from text inputs, yielding significant improvements in model performance compared to simulated interactions. To produce realistic simulations at a rate of one million steps per second, our method involves a customized text-based game environment called TextWorldExpress. It generates text-based puzzles by dynamically creating rules and state conditions, resulting in natural language puzzles that enable efficient scaling of simulated training data. The environment successfully achieves a simulation rate of 25,000 puzzles per second, and when integrated with fast neural network architectures, it can simulate an entire puzzle every three milliseconds. To validate our approach, we compared the performance of three neural model types on both the TextWorld and TextWorldExpress game environments. The results showed that the implemented changes in TextWorldExpress maintain puzzle solving accuracy comparable to the original TextWorld environment at a matching code efficiency level, while producing a 74-fold improvement in training efficiency and a 19-fold reduction in end-to-end latency per puzzle.

Topological insulators exhibiting defects have been found to have unique properties, and their mathematical representation using C^*-algebras and K-theory has been established.  Specifically, a compact space representing the defect was found to be isomorphic to the 1-skeleton of the Eilenberg-Moore category for commutative C^*-algebras and continuous functions, which has the property of being homologically equivalent to the 1-skeleton of the Stiefel manifold. As a non-trivial application, a new model of the Dirac operator on the 1-skeleton of the Stiefel manifold is proposed.

Consider a sector in the plane defined by a small angle $\alpha$, less than $\frac{7}{18}$. We investigate the behavior of $p$-harmonic functions, where $p$ is greater than 2, within this sector, focusing on the scenario where the function's gradient is notably small, specifically less than $\epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is a sufficiently small value. Under these constraints, we demonstrate that the maximum function value at distance $r$ from the sector's vertex does not grow faster than the product of the angle $\alpha$ and the distance $r$. Moreover, our proof relies on the discovery of a specific type of function, or $\Phi$-seminorm, to establish the existence of a linear-based Taylor expansion for $p$-harmonic functions in a sector with angle $\alpha$ and curvature $\beta$, where both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ adhere to strict upper bounds.

Identifying the joint probability of the lowest barometric pressure and highest wind speed is crucial in analyzing extreme weather patterns, particularly for assessing the severity of hurricanes. This study builds upon previous research in extreme weather analysis by introducing innovative statistical models for examining the relationship between low-pressure systems and high wind speeds, corresponding to Category 3 hurricanes. The authors propose a range of copula models based on extreme value theory, which can be used to study the frequency of intense wind storms. These copula models are supplemented by a measurement of dependence known as the exchangeability index. The research involves an in-depth analysis of data collected from the North Atlantic between 1979 and 2015, by combining satellite information and numerical weather forecasts to simulate wind fields and locate low-pressure centers. The simulated data follows a multivariate extreme value distribution, which the authors show can be represented by a mixture model consisting of a finite number of multivariate extremes. The study compares various exchangeability indices and joint probability distributions to evaluate the accuracy of low-pressure system frequency estimates, by evaluating how well they match observed data. The results reveal that no single model perfectly fits the observed data, but a combination of two groups of probabilities best approximates the observed patterns.

Inspired by work of Ulmer, where theulertupleconjecture proved the finitude of non-constant maps from an overlocalfield to an elliptic curve over aglobalfield, we consider the faustelconjecture where the target elliptic curve is defined over a overlocalfield instead of aglobalfield. Moreover, where theulertupleconjecture used derhamcohomology to establish faustelconjecture, we employ a similar method in proving a general version of faustelconjecture where both the faustelconjecture and its elliptic curve special case can be reduced to showing finitude of non-constant maps over an overlocalfield when the faustelconjecture holds for all curves over aglobalfield.

In the field of human-robot collaborative manipulation, a robot's manipulator workspace and a human's reach workspace can be visually represented using corresponding colors that indicate feasible and infeasible areas for each. The intersection of these workspaces is known as the manipulability domain, a domain of significance in manipulation tasks. This domain can be visually analyzed by physically moving a robot and capturing 3D point clouds of the intersection area. However, this method is time-consuming and requires specialized equipment to combine the captured data. This paper presents a novel digital approach to estimating the manipulability domain by transferring a synthesized intersection point cloud from a robot frame to a human-robot system frame. This is achieved through a proposed method that involves a frame transformation and alignment technique utilizing an advanced algorithm. The matrix element method, specifically its differential versions, offers a comparative advantage in analyzing finite decay width effects in Higgs boson pair production compared to on-shell production assumptions. We investigate the validity of treating the Higgs boson pairs as resonant production processes at the LHC, taking into account the non-resonant Higgs boson production through virtual intermediate states involving the decay channel Higgs boson pair $\to$ b anti-b two-Wi, using next-to-leading order (NLO) calculations across the relevant energy range of the LHC.

A novel training approach is proposed that utilizes real-world data, specifically images from sensors real-world cameras, to generate accurate 3D object representations and their orientations. Unlike existing benchmark datasets that rely on labeled data, this method utilizes actual rotating objects to create a comprehensive dataset for 3D object recognition. Specifically, this work develops a system called Accidental Turntables (AT) that captures real-world images of turning objects using regular 2D images, and learns to create accurate 3D models and their orientations using a network. This approach was tested on several types of objects, including everyday items, vehicles, and challenging categories like aircraft, and the results show that the generated 3D models are accurate and can be used for 3D object recognition. Furthermore, the validity and reliability of the proposed approach were verified using quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics. Finally, the proposed approach was used to train two popular 3D object recognition models, Shape Index (SHNet) and PointNet, and the results show that these models achieve state-of-the-art performance levels on benchmark datasets.

The rapid spread of false COVID-19 vaccine information on social media has a detrimental effect on public health, with many people falling victim to the distortion of factual data. To tackle this issue, we aim to understand how vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals react to misinformation on Twitter during pandemic times. By examining unmoderated forums, our research explores the distinct response patterns of these two groups towards various types of misinformation spread by both vaccinated and non-vaccinated individuals. To achieve this, we introduce our dataset of nearly 340,000 retweets from unmoderated Facebook groups in the United States spanning from January 2021 to March 2022. By analyzing this data, our understanding of how different groups perceive and react to misinformation will be deepened, ultimately informing more effective fact-checking and counter-misinformation strategies.

A highly-isolated attosecond pulse train is produced through the interference of two opposite-color laser pulses within the extreme environment of an argon plasma. The frequency of the generated pulses can be precisely controlled by the intensity of the background laser, as demonstrated by the model's numerical simulation. By leveraging the non-linear properties of the plasma and the equilibrium condition of the argon plasma, our source offers an advantage over traditional coherent attosecond pulse sources in terms of its output.

Recent observations from the Gaia mission have identified several potential examples of interactive binary systems among non interacting Algol-type eclipsing binaries. We analyzed a set of 172 such candidates out of 5363 identified by the Gaia Data Release 3 catalog. Using Gaia's astrometric ASTROM solutions and photometric data, we examined candidates that showed signs of a possible second companion star. We found significant evidence for hidden binary companions in 17 Algol-type objects and applied mass estimation techniques to assess the potential partners. We also identified objects requiring further study due to the possibility of masquerading binary systems. These objects require further study with photometry and spectroscopy to verify the presence of hidden companions and understand the objects dynamics. Our analysis also included mass estimation for the potential partners and we found that the mass of the less massive primary component could be within a certain range.
