Insulating magnetic order exists in pyrochlore iridate (A_2Ir_2O_7) series, 
where semi-filled 5d states of Ir4+ interact with the lattice to create magnetically 
ordered insulating phases. By replacing Eu with Bi in (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir_2O_7, a tuning 
tool is utilized to transition the material from a stable insulating magnetic phase 
to a theorized QSL phase by increasing the spin-orbit coupling to angular momentum 
ratio and weakening the lattice coupling through expansion. Experimental analysis 
using HAXPES and theoretical DFT and band structure calculations confirm the 
material undergoes a transition from an insulator to metal based on Bi 
concentration by increasing the 5d electronic state occupancy at the Fermi level.

This review examines the concepts of the core and interior of a set in relation to a product space component structure, specifically focusing on a 2-dimensional set-valued mapping. We provide a comprehensive analysis of these concepts through established results that connect them to a property known as horizontal strict differential regularity. We also discuss alternative definitions of the core's interior and present efficient algorithms for calculating them, which rely on properties of 2-by-2 determinants. These selections can then be extended to valuations on partitional spaces, which have properties similar to Lipschitz continuity. We specifically highlight the development of selection algorithms for Lipschitz-type mappings, including an example of horizontal strict differential regularity and a corresponding Lipschitz-type mapping, showing how a corresponding setValued map has a corresponding selection with a specific property.

This paper, in relation to the likelihood principle, refers to sets of models as "likelihoods" to distinguish them from statistical experiments, which also adhere to the likelihood principle. A specific type of likelihood, known as a cyclic likelihood, has been defined. It's characterized by the existence of a sequence of models where each model admits significant evidence, known as strong-likelihood support, for the next model in the sequence. All cyclic likelihoods possess the property of being nontransitive, meaning there exist models A, B, and C such that model A admits strong-likelihood support for model B, model B for model C, but model A admits strong-likelihood support for model A. Furthermore, there exist examples of continuous, symmetric, univariate likelihoods that are nontransitive, in contrast to multivariate normal likelihoods, which are always transitive.

Certain software systems require Run-time Setup Space (RSS) to be defined at execution time, but doing so within the constraints of dynamic environments often proves difficult and inefficient. Alternately, programmers can predeterminedly define parts of the RSS at compile-time. Though this approach simplifies maintenance and increases reliability, it eliminates the system's adaptability to different environments. Our research focuses on enabling a degree of compile-time RSS customization while still allowing some run-time adjustment. Our proposal targets a subset of C++ where the exact composition of the RSS must be defined either at execution time or compilation, providing insights into feasible solutions.

Particles of dark matter interacting via nuclear forces can transfer a significant amount of energy to electrons within a nucleus, making a direct detection possible even for sub-GeV dark matter particles. By setting a lower bound on the probability of dark matter particles being found in a particular state, researchers can establish a detection limit that reflects this concept in a direct way. Consideration is also given to the variation in the strength of dark matter forces depending on the type of particle involved and over varying distance scales.

The anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, an extension of the Jaynes-Cummings interaction that includes both excitation and de-excitation processes, is explored where a two-level atom interacts with a single-mode quantum field. By examining the temporal evolution of the system under different initial conditions, Rabi oscillations and field-atom entanglement dynamics are found to be comparable to those observed in the standard Jaynes-Cummings model. However, interest in the JCM continues to grow due to its broad applications in quantum information science. This has led to increased study of the interaction between quantum systems and optical fields for generating optical nonclassicality and quantum correlations. This exposure has sparked investigation into modifications of the JCM and its applications in entanglement and state transfer. One such generalization is the anti-JC model, where a two-level atom interacts with a quantum field by exchanging excitations only when the atom is in its ground state. In this context, we examine the temporal dynamics of Rabi oscillations and entanglement in the anti-JC model and investigate its potential for transmitting quantum correlations and entanglement. Our analysis indicates that the anti-JC model can facilitate growing entanglement and transmit quantum correlations effectively, even exhibiting nonlocal deterministic quantum switchover between the atom and field without switchover delay.

Nonlinear dynamics in physiological data can be quantified by measuring time intervals in cardiac and brain electrical signals. One such measurement, the inter-beat interval (IBI), can reveal how the heart responds to different states, such as rest, exercise, and emotional changes. Various models have been proposed to estimate IBIs from noisy signals, but their effectiveness can be limited by errors in peak detection and variable noise levels. This study presents a two-step method for IBI estimation that addresses these challenges. Initially, a peak detection algorithm is used to identify local maxima in the signal, resulting in rough estimations of IBIs. These estimations are then refined by a deep neural network based on the Tiramisu model, which is trained to accurately train IBI estimates. The approach was tested on Apnea-Link data and demonstrated a 16.6% reduction in IBI estimation error compared to existing models.

We assess the work fluctuation dynamics in a diverse set of active particles by examining the over-damped version of the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in various spatial dimensions and under multiple types of forces. These forces include linear restoring forces, non-conservative forces proportional to activity, a restoring force with an activity-dependent magnitude, and a non-conservative force of magnitude proportional to activity that varies with the first order of position. Our results in these models yield exact free energy distributions, which we verify against the generalized Crooks theorem in the third and a generalised Jarzynski theorem in the first order of activity. Moreover, our findings show significant discrepancies in the scaling of average work variation with time for the models with linear and non-linear restoring forces, and we identify the underlying causes for these differences.

Gesture recognition is a complex area where humans excel but current computer systems fall short. The primary obstacle in computer gesture recognition is the lack of a comprehensive, diverse dataset with multiple viewpoints of hand and body movements. To overcome this limitation, we've developed HUMBI, a large-scale multiview dataset featuring annotated hand and body movements across 22 views for 65 distinct gestures performed by 12 individuals wearing sensors to accurately capture all hand positions. Utilizing HUMBI in our benchmark challenge revealed the effectiveness of our approach, particularly our use of a multiview point cloud fusion and a novel architecture, yielding impressive results in view prediction and gesture recognition tasks.

Our goal is to develop universal neural models capable of handling tasks across various languages, and to do so, we design representations that provide subtle influence over model output, rather than acting as the primary training mechanism. Initially, our approach involves training these representations in a supervised environment, but we discover that they primarily replicate model behavior, offering minimal improvement. In response, we introduce a new technique that allows them to learn task-specific features independently of the existing model, introducing a modest but meaningful modification to the model's predictions. Initially trained models are found to offer an upper limit to this correction. Ultimately, by incorporating their structure into a pre-training method, we achieve significant performance gains for base models across multiple languages without requiring extensive multi-task training. Notably, our pre-trained model, combined with representations, delivers state-of-the-art results on the NLTK benchmark, surpassing current models that are highly dependent on pre-training. Additionally, we examine the effect of representations as a post-hoc model refinement method, achieving considerable improvements on tasks processed within a single language context.

A prevalent approach in video super-resolution is the BVS framework, which leverages spatial-temporal alignment and propagation to simplify the task. A critical component of BVS is the alignment module, where recurrent neural networks have been the dominant choice due to their sequential nature that facilitates alignment. However, our analysis reveals that the stacked recurrent units used in BVS may hinder the efficient flow of gradients during gradient back-propagation, leading to poor convergence and degraded super-resolution results. Building on this insight, we introduce the BasicVSR framework, which optimizes the design of the alignment module to improve gradient flow-Backpropagation. Specifically, we propose using bidirectional recurrent units within the alignment module to accelerate convergence. Furthermore, we incorporate multi-scale features into the alignment module to boost the quality of the video super-resolution results. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the quality of video super-resolution in comparison to state-of-the-art methods by achieving superior PSNR and SSIM scores on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

To effectively learn an accurate environment model in reinforcement learning, multiple tasks are required to avoid biases that arise from a limited range of experiences. This study examines how multi-task learning is affected by model representation, and discovers that a common network architecture suffers from interference across tasks, which significantly hinders performance and leads to the complete failure of learning in some cases. However, a modular network setup, comprising distinct sub-networks for each task, demonstrates superior stability and enhanced performance compared to its single-network counterpart. This study contributes to the understanding of multi-task learning in reinforcement learning by contributing a dataset of 7 tasks from continuous and multi-dimensional discrete action spaces, along with the new finding that modular networks outperform single-network models.

We examine the performance of thermal machines operating over finite timeframes, subject to limitations on their control variables. For scenarios involving non-reversible control constraints, we develop criteria for optimizing power output and provide a mathematical framework - specifically the maximum principle - to determine the optimal trajectory of states, durations, and control parameters. Our analysis encompasses various durations, and within certain restricted parameters, we demonstrate the existence of exponentially decaying functions that converge to optimal durations, thus confirming the existence of optimal operating points for these constrained machines.

To analyze the spatial consequences of historical hurricanes and storm surges on power systems, a model was developed that utilizes power lines as leading edges and integrates real-time geospatial data with standard power system simulation tools. This approach enables precise modeling of hurricane paths and storm surge impacts, which can be used to assess power outages during historical hurricanes.
This study introduces a novel approach based on Clifford analysis to establish a three balls conjecture for the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator.

We're analyzing specific versions of the heterochaos baker map in two dimensions, focusing on an invariant line with an attracting property. This area of study connects to the broader investigation of partially hyperbolic systems featuring a stable one-dimensional direction. The document initially explores a family of heterochaos baker maps in the context of a dynamical system introduced by Collet and Varrault. By solving for the unique invariant probability measure with a maximal entropy component along a stable manifold, we establish the existence of an invariant sigma-algebra with a specific property. This measure is found to reside on a complex manifold with an intricate fractal structure. The breakdown of accessibility to this measure results from the presence of an uncountable collection of sets with probability zero. The article later extends this analysis to generalizing this map in two dimensions while maintaining the properties of stable/unstable foliations.

Our focus is on extended Higgs sectors in relation to the muon anomaly, with particular interest in the scenario where $\sin \beta = 1$. We examine the expanded Higgs sector's impact on collider signatures and colliding beam energy requirements to detect the additional states present. The investigation encompasses the scientific prospects of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), potential coliders like the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), and a range of electron-positron colliding facilities including ILC, CLIC, and CIRCÉ.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), which enhances the performance of the existing WaveNet model through the integration of pitch-adaptive dilated convolution neural networks and a pitch-dependent skip connection architecture, all aimed at efficiently modeling the repetitive nature of speech and sound. The proposed model's simplicity allows it to be trained directly on raw speech waveforms, which results in improved speech synthesis quality over the existing models, as demonstrated by the lower values of the Mean-Square Error and the Multi-Fréchet Intra-Class Distance (WOSM OSI) metrics in the speech synthesis evaluation. The quality of the synthesized speech was further optimized through the implementation of the predicted duration refinement module and the proposed model was successfully applied in the task of speech-upscaling. The source code of the model is available online at the repository link (https://github.com/Georgi-Kirov/quasi-periodic-wavenet).

One of the significant benefits of Collaborative Recommendation (CR) lies in its capacity to analyze user behavior patterns. Nevertheless, conventional Collaborative Recommendation approaches often fail when dealing with highly subjective and sparse datasets characterized by diverse and idiosyncratic user preferences. To address this shortcoming, this study proposes a user-tailored biclustering-based Collaborative Recommendation method capable of accommodating user-specific preferences. This model categorizes users into clusters based on the locality of their preferences, utilizes biclusters to identify and exploit related items within user behavior data, and recommends items based on bicluster leaders and user requirements. Extensive evaluations conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in enhancing the accuracy of recommendations and its ability to handle preference locality, sparsity, and subjectivity simultaneously. Moreover, this studyTies the BCR model's performance closely to that of users' bicluster leaders and shows that its efficacy grows as preferences become more homogeneous.

Precise knowledge of the sun's activity and its properties is essential for understanding the disk-integrated observations made by instruments such as HARPS-N solar mode. By employing a high-resolution, high-resolution spectrograph HARPS-N was able to create a high-resolution data set of the sun's activity, and, in order to do so, it used line bisector measures (LBS) of Fe I absorption lines, which are commonly used to detect solar activity. Furthermore, it employs the S-index to measure chromospheric activity and the H-alpha central reversal degree (ARD) to track solar activity in the chromosphere. Our research involved the examination of a substantial data set of the sun's activity, which was made possible by the HARPS-N's observations during 2015-2019. Using a large-line width data set of the sun's absorption lines, it enables the comparison of the sun's activity with terrestrial data of the sun's activity. Our findings show a significant correlation of the sun's activity on an 11-year cycle in its LBS measurements and the H-alpha and CaH266.6 central reversal degree measurements. Additionally, our results show a 10-day time lag of the LBS and a 15-day time lag of the H-alpha and CaH266.6 central reversal degree, and the S-index measurements behind the sun's spots before the sun's spots and the H-alpha and CaH266

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana fermions and other causes, we have developed an innovative method employing an electrically conductive electrode in tunneling spectroscopy experiments. When a non-Majorana zero-energy peak is formed through the interaction of four Dirac fermions, the resistance of the electrode causes the feature in the second-order differential conductance graph to fade as resistance increases, whereas Majorana fermions produce a distinct signal characterized by an amplitude directly related to the electrode's resistance.

The concept of shadows in one area of mathematics has proven useful in 
guiding researchers towards the correct higher-categorical framework in 
lower-categorical contexts. This note extends that guidance by showing the 
way to bicategories is through bicategorical shadows.

We introduce the first pair of convolutional networks capable of learning a thorough style, enabling a seamless conversion between images with opposite color tones. These networks operate by mapping original images to their altered counterparts, providing a reliable method to obtain images with double red color components and normalizing them back to a color tone of 0. Our proposed style is particularly effective for its simplicity, requiring minimal data for acquisition (i.e., images with varied color tones). Furthermore, we explore the notion of incorporating image pairs into the normalization process to prevent data distortion, distinct from the standard data normalization employed in current network training procedures. Our experiments validate the superiority of our handcrafted and pair-based style over the utilization of pre-trained models from external datasets for achieving accurate double red color conversion and image recovery.

This technical report showcases the specifics of our model employed in the CVE
track of the AQTC challenge at CVPR 2022. The model integrates a CNN architecture
with a hybrid loss function, combining classification and envelope regression losses.
It also features a data augmentation technique that modifies images based on
contextual cues.  The rationale behind our model and its corresponding
implementations are detailed within this report.

In a controlled laboratory setting, the settling of snow particles in the atmosphere under turbulent and non-snowing conditions is examined. By utilizing a localized heat source to simulate atmospheric turbulence, the movement of snow particles is observed to be predominantly controlled by drag forces when their size is small. For snow particles smaller than 200 micrometers, vertical movement is limited to less than 10 millimeters before their trajectory shifts to a horizontal path. When the hydrodynamic forces exceed the buoyancy forces, these particles are rapidly swept in the direction of the wind at a distance greater than 10 centimeters from the source. The observed threshold for this transition aligns with the theoretical model of the critical particle diameter, denoted as $d_c$. The distribution of these snow particles in the atmosphere forms an inverted pyramid shape, with their movement analyzed through the theoretical frameworks of a parabolic airfoil and a theoretical theoretical model of critical particle diameter. The snow particles with a diameter of approximately 150 micrometers exhibit an average travel distance of around 17 centimeters, after which they are rapidly swept in the direction of the wind.

This paper explores a novel approach to active learning, which utilizes deep reinforcement learning to identify the most informative data points for robot navigation within a3D environment.  A convolutional neural network based model is developed that depends on current and anticipated sensor inputs to determine when a data point is sufficient and the current robot position should be added to the training set.  Our approach differs from the state of the art in several aspects, particularly in enabling active learning without the requirement of labeling, allowing it to function effectively with imperfect data, and enabling it to be combined with imitation learning to provide enhanced starting points.  Experiments were conducted using a physical robot to demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in several tasks including home building for navigation and home following, and we observed improvements of up to 50% in the robot's home detection accuracy compared to conventional methods based on uniform sampling.

Effective vertex finding in high-energy physics experiments hinges on the capability of sparse 3D grids to track particle trajectories with precision. As particle collision events increase in number, the computational burden of processing 3D data sets rises, necessitating more efficient methods of computation. This study proposes an innovative approach to reduce sparse 3D data sets using a novel network architecture known as Bicephalous Convolutional Autoencoder (BCAE), which not only compresses the data set but also ensures high-quality reconstruction. Consequently, this reduction in size facilitates accelerated sparse matrix operations, thereby enhancing computational speed. By employing BCAE, a 4x-20x reduction in the volume of 3D data sets is achieved, while simultaneously, training and inference times are reduced by up to 4x and 20x respectively. Moreover, improved BCAEs yield better performance than existing optimization methods in terms of both reconstruction quality and the accuracy of sparse matrix operations. These results are particularly significant as they specifically address the efficient computation of sparse 3D data sets, distinguishing themselves from other sparse matrix computation techniques.

Our analysis reveals the effects of the Finzi gravity model on the distribution of galactic clusters across the universe. The research focuses on the number of galactic clusters as a function of their density contrast. Compared to Newtonian dynamics, the positive branch of the Finzi model's prediction shows a significant divergence, particularly at large values of the w parameter. However, for small values of w, the number of clusters follows the 5/3 power law. In contrast, the negative branch of the Finzi model yields a linear relationship between the number of clusters and their density contrast. Furthermore, the research identifies specific ranges for the scaling exponent of the Finzi model for both the positive and negative branches.

A geometric hypergraph can be defined using a set of geometric objects, where each edge represents a collection of objects that are connected through intersection at a common point. Researchers have explored the concept of saturation with respect to a configuration of type $(s, k)$ - where $s$ points converge and $k$ edges meet at a point. They discovered that there exists a threshold $t_{(s, k)}$ where above which any large enough convex hypergraph containing no $(s, k)$-configuration is completely disconnected. This threshold is known to lie within the range $[t_{(s, 1)} , t_{(s, 2)}]$, where values of $t_{(s, j)}$ are known. However, the upper bound for this threshold is now proven to be lower, at $\min\{ bs^3, C \cdot s^2 \cdot b\}$. Where $b$ is the number of hypergraph edges, and $C$ is a constant, showing that below this threshold such hypergraphs contain many geometric objects, showing their convexity.

To study the inclusive alpha energy spectrum of the 6Li + 51V collision, a theoretical model was employed and its validity was verified through comparison with experimental data from the 6Li + 54Fe system. Application of this model to the 6Li + 51V collision reveals both direct and composite nuclear reaction contributions, with the former dominating at higher energy levels and lower angular positions, and the latter mainly contributing at lower energy levels and higher angular positions. Notably, the compound nuclear reaction mainly originates from the 38Ar excited states.

This research introduces a novel robotic system designed to mimic the locomotion of Pacific Lamprey, an ancient vertebrate known for its unique feeding and climbing techniques. A key focus of this study is on developing exoskeletal control methods that replicate the Pacific Lamprey's locomotion while also exploring how to adapt its exoskeletal control for a rigid robot body. The resulting research has yielded two innovative exoskeletal control strategies tailored to Pacific Lamprey's specific movements. A simulation has been created to accurately model Pacific Lamprey locomotion, which has been used to evaluate the performance and versatility of these exoskeletal control strategies.

This study formulates a framework for optimizing treatments in a cancer model affected by random disturbances. The cancer development in individuals is represented by a stochastic process in a 2D space influenced by random noise. For optimizing therapies in such a noise-prone environment, we utilize the Fokker-Planck framework. Our objective is to enhance patient survival and quality of life by employing an optimal treatment intensity in the form of an immune system booster. To achieve this, we minimize cancer presence and its uniform distribution across the body using the first and second moments of the probability density function, respectively. Our analysis reveals that achieving cancer reduction often results in concentrated cell populations, suggesting that optimal treatments should focus on minimizing variance rather than mean cancer distribution. Our numerical results reveal that certain levels of random noise prevent the creation of optimal treatments, implying that further research is necessary to develop robust and personalized treatments in highly variable environments.

The increasing importance of data reliability and timeliness in wireless D2D communication systems has led to a growing interest in the age of information (AoI) as a metric for measuring the freshness of data. However, minimizing the AoI in mobile D2D systems is complicated due to various factors such as data accumulation, transmission scheduling, and message updates. In this paper, we explore a D2D-enhanced cellular network where the source randomly modifies its data and the D2D nodes forward the messages in a multi-hop fashion until the age of the data at the source changes again. Based on this network setup, a two-step scheme is proposed to minimize the AoI: first, the performance analysis of the network is examined to derive the average AoI in terms of system parameters; second, a two-step optimization strategy is designed to find the optimal message forwarding and source update policies by applying the least-squares method and a deep reinforcement learning technique. The results show that this optimization strategy achieves better results compared to a conventional power allocation method in terms of minimizing the AoI.

The reflective property at an infinite wave number in the dispersion relation is seen in dBSII equations with variable coefficients and the Daleckii-Istomov reflection principle was proven under specific conditions. However, at an infinite wave number, the reflection coefficient's behavior is generally seen to be more widespread across the two dBSII equations.

Current gravitational-wave detectors have limitations in detecting subtle deviations from circular orbits in merging compact objects. To address this, we've developed an analytical model that accurately estimates how orbital distortions evolve over time for masses within the range of detector capabilities. Our findings reveal that at least one parameter must be known to within 10% to predict detector thresholds with 10% accuracy. However, using well-established binary black-hole parameters from numerical simulations significantly minimizes uncertainties. We observe that lower mass ratios and larger distances from detectors result in greater errors in detecting eccentricities. For instance, the most sensitive detectors might miss signals due to insufficient resolution of subtle orbital distortions. Our study also reveals that detector capabilities vary based on how many waves can be resolved during an inspiral. Essentially, detecting systems at more distant thresholds allows for better observation of multiple waves, thereby reducing uncertainties. Our analysis reveals that even slight inaccuracies in estimating the characteristic frequency can have substantial impacts on detector performance, potentially leading to deviations of over 200% for certain scenarios.

A proposed X-ray amplifier built around the Cornell Linear Collider (CLIC) based Free-Electron Laser ( FEL) oscillator holds the potential to be a groundbreaking source of high-power, intense X-ray pulses at specific wavelengths between 4 and 12 nanometers. By utilizing an electron collider as the optical pump for a CLIC-FEL oscillator, the design could achieve capabilities far exceeding current free-electron laser systems, with gains as high as $10^{10}$ percent and power in the gigawatt range. Employing a dual-pass configuration allows for amplification in the presence of substantial gain while mitigating drawbacks such as saturation and self-amplitude modulation effects, overcoming limitations of traditional single-pass schemes and enabling new possibilities in nonlinear X-ray processes and the study of complex physical phenomena.

Dynamic graph incidents often trigger disruptions in online social networks and can spread rapidly, yet incident-induced disruptions have been under-researched in graph data mining. A novel type of dynamic graph anomaly called "incident" is proposed, characterized by a cluster of connected nodes that exhibit disrupted, semi-isolated behavior, distinguishing it from time-series data anomalies. Incident detection on dynamic graphs is an复杂 task, hindered by the sparse and unbalanced distribution of data across different time steps. A novel framework, specifically designed for identifying incidents on dynamic graphs, is presented. It effectively aggregates time-series data and multiple incidents into a unified structure, to prevent potential information loss. A novel framework for learning on the constructed data matrix is also proposed, with the objective of flagging potential incidents on dynamic graphs. Extensive experiments are carried out to demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance on a synthetic dataset.

High-energy astrophysical phenomena such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts are widely believed to originate from the intense radiation emitted during the collapse of massive stars. These events, including supernovae and bursts, are thought to be powered by massive stellar cores that undergo catastrophic implosion. The study of such stellar explosions is complicated by the vast range of time scales involved, spanning from the seconds of the final shock outbreak to the years followed by the outburst. The simulations of these events are particularly challenging due to the need for high spatial resolution in the areas close to the collapsing star, while the outflow regions can be modeled with significantly less precision. The analyses of peninsulas in the pressure profile are critical in revealing the early dynamics of these events, although their identification is hindered by computational limitations. The research presented here focuses on the formation and evolution of final shock waves in massive stellar cores following a catastrophic implosion. The study involves high-resolution simulations of the core region and compares them to lower-resolution models of the outflow. The results reveal the intricate processes involved in both the implosion and subsequent outflow, including the growth of instability in the outer layers, growth of turbulent energy, and growth of final shock. The study provides a detailed examination of the final shock's behavior and compares it to the expected patterns in super-Novae and in other massive stellar collapses.

The increasing dependence on Artificial Intelligence (AI) across various sectors has led to significant interest in its explainability. Understandability of AI systems is crucial for building trust with end-users, making this a key focus area in many industries. Understanding the concept of explainability within the context of requirements engineering and its understanding is essential to its effective implementation. As a relative newcomer in the field of requirements engineering, there is a need to integrate it with field-specific knowledge to develop a comprehensive understanding. In the following discussion, we aim to contribute in two key ways: firstly, by offering support to researchers in understanding and managing the complexities of explainability requirements through modern techniques, and secondly, by encouraging them to explore new possibilities in the field of responsible artificial intelligence by leveraging the capabilities of requirements engineering.

The detection of abnormal growths within the colon, such as polyps, during colonoscopy examinations necessitates expert examination of collected tissue samples by pathologists. To improve diagnostic accuracy, computer-aided systems can be trained to support pathologists in analyzing histological slides. To develop these systems, we have created an open dataset named UniToPatho. This dataset consists of annotated and whole-slide histological images, along with corresponding labels from expert pathologists for identifying colorectal polyps adenoma grading. UniToPatho's annotation process involved over 2000 hours of work by more than 10 technicians and was supplemented by in-house segmentation tools. This dataset will facilitate research in computer-assisted histological slide analysis.

In modern source coding, zero-error schemes are employed to prevent information leakage during the coding process.  Graph theory has become an essential mathematical tool for analyzing these schemes, particularly in determining the zero-error rate and the minimum redundancy required for coding.  This work aims to explore how key graph characteristics influence the zero-error schemes' key attributes, such as split error and residue, which respectively measure incorrect transmissions and premature termination.  By establishing theoretical bounds on split error and residue based on these graph characteristics, we gain insight into how they impact performance.  This analysis ultimately leads to the proposal of new indicators for evaluating split error and residue, providing graph-theoretic bounds specific to particular graph classes.

Deep learning methods have shown great potential for enhancing Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images, which are often hampered by low resolution and high noise levels. Solved individually, current approaches however fall short of producing novel images with reduced noise. In this study, we present a novel hierarchical generative model, called MrSAR, which can generate realistic and detailed radar images based on low-resolution inputs or even just a single image, accompanied by optional control parameters for specified features such as object count and type. Our results with these models reveal that the high-quality images produced by MrAR are superior to current method in producing in-painting, super-in-resolution, and in-noise reduction effects, indicating its applicability in novel image generation for the above applications.

The Quantum Approximation Optimization Algorithm uses a specific quantum state to solve optimization problems by providing a approximate solution with guaranteed quality.  As an important indicator, a parameter related to the problem's minimum energy is incorporated in the state.  Finding these parameters through traditional methods is complex and time-consuming due to their connection with non-linear equations and a significant dependence on the problem's nature.  To address this issue, a new approach based on Bayesian optimization has been developed to efficiently determine the parameters using a combination of experimentation and theoretical analysis.

A precise mathematical formula has been developed for calculating the area where two elliptical shapes intersect. The complexity of this problem lies in the fact that there's no closed-form solution for calculating the region within an arbitrary ellipse, but it can be approximated using its segment area, and the intersection region can be broken down into multiple sub-segments or defined by its boundary. To tackle this, we developed a computationally efficient method that involves numerically finding the intersection points of the two ellipses, which results in up to eight points, and the overall time complexity is O(d), where 'd' represents the depth of the recursive function used to calculate the area, and for most cases, 'd' does not exceed four. The intersection area can then be calculated in a constant amount of time, making our algorithm potentially optimal. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our solution's runtime, despite being potentially optimal, does not exceed other existing algorithms for polygon-based area calculations.

The q-Learning algorithm has gained recognition for its ability to handle continuous action spaces, yet it has been criticized for employing a suboptimal discretization technique known as the Lattice Method. This document validates previous concerns by demonstrating that q-Learning, when applied with the Lattice Method, fails with constant time step discretizations and yields inconsistent results with varying grid sizes. In an effort to address these issues, this document explores the Aligned Lattice Method, which can achieve convergence for SARQ, QBDS, and TBDS reinforcement learning operators when carefully chosen. However, the requirements for aligned operators significantly reduce the size of applicable state-action spaces. As a result, this work develops a strategy for estimating the state-action queue, which adapts its size depending on the applicable state-action space. This adaptive approach ensures that q-Learning can converge for environments with relatively low applicable state-action spaces and remains stable across discretizations, although the associated operator is non-symmetric.

Our research is centered on an extended triangular lattice Hubbard model which incorporates next-nearest neighbor interactions into consideration. By exploring the anti-doped regime of this model, we utilized numerical methods, specifically a full full configuration interaction quantum Monte Carlo approach, to analyze the ground states for various values of the coupling constants t, t', and U. The study focuses on the effect of a specifically configured t', (-1.5t) in the absence of additional coupling, which shows an order of local magnetic moments similar to the triangular-lattice Heisenberg model with the same coupling, but with a localized moment size reduction of approximately 20%. We observe that this order decays in a power of distance from the anti-ferromagnetic point. Moreover, we demonstrate that this order is preserved at very high energy levels of the coupling, but causes a metal to insulator transition, which is in sharp contrast to the usual electron localization that results in the pored regime of the doped triangular lattice. Furthermore, we show that this order decays in a power of distance from the Neel state, which is in agreement with various predictions. Moreover, we found that the order is not disrupted by the introduction of additional coupling, but by utilizing our approach, we found that the order is not disrupted by the introduction of additional coupling, but by utilizing our approach, we found that the order is not disrupted by the introduction of additional coupling.

Accurate vertebrae identification is crucial for various medical image tasks, like medical image segmentation and image registration. In this paper, we develop an innovative technique that leverages deep learning and rectification in the anterior-posterior direction of CT scans to identify vertebrae boundaries. This approach employs a rectification module, trained using deep neural networks, to correct the anatomy of CT scans and facilitate anatomical convolutional neural network-based detection functions. A specific loss function is designed to streamline anatomical convolution operations, and a specialized anatomical optimization module is developed to accelerate vertebrae detection functions. Extensive experiments on the public spine CT dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Comparative analysis shows that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a mean identification accuracy of 99.06% and a mean absolute error of 1.02 cm for vertebrae detection. These outcomes indicate that our method has the potential to accelerate and enhance the effectiveness of automated vertebra localization and identification systems.

The quantum Hilbert scheme for a toric variety efficiently encapsulates all possible quantizations of the corresponding semi-classual coherent sheaf. We investigate how the geometry of the quantized rational surface evolves when the underlying semi-classical sheaf undergoes a birational transformation. Our research reveals that the quantized surface corresponding to the quantized projective plane exhibits an isomorphic structure, which explicitly breaks symmetry under such a transformation, in contrast to the classical Riemann sphere which remains invariant. Similarly, the quantized affine plane also displays this discrete, non-invariant behavior. While the quantized Hurwitz space and the quantized moduli space also exhibit a clear breakdown of continuous symmetries under such transformations, the quantum Hilbert scheme for the quantized Fano threefold with a continuous isometric family does not exhibit this discrete non-isomorphism characteristic.

Our study explores the full transmission of acoustic energy in pairs of piezoelectric crystals in close proximity, originating from one detector and being completely captured by its neighboring unit. This phenomenon is exemplified by two interconnected lithium niobate crystals. The transmission is facilitated by the exchange of surface phonon-polaritons across the interface, as well as by a resonant mechanical movement triggered by the activation of a specific force field along the axis perpendicular to the interface. The observed transmission is significantly higher than what theoretical models suggest should be possible through radiation mechanisms alone, and is highly dependent on the alignment of the crystals along particular directional axes.

Non-equilibrium systems that form dense states through thermal or dynamic processes have great potential for applications in photonic circuits. This thesis investigates the creation of all-optical systems, known as reservoirs, that support these dense states and the design of novel devices based on this principle. The study begins with an analysis of a reservoir system containing organic microcrystals that become superluminescent when excited above a certain threshold of power. Next, I present a theoretical model for a new method to achieve polariton condensation at lower energies. Furthermore, I propose a research approach to develop room temperature superconductors using polariton condensation in materials with two bands of electrons. Finally, I propose a research direction for creating room temperature lasers based on polariton condensation in materials with delayed feedback.

The rapid evaporation of exoplanets like K2-22 b creates a flow of tiny particles that leave the planet's surface, allowing scientists to study its composition using light signals. A research team used observations from the Two Telescope Array and the LBT to analyze starlight passing through K2-22 b's escaping atmosphere, discovering evidence of large particles up to 0.45 microns in size. Analyzing the effects on different wavelengths revealed a substantial mass loss rate evaporation around 10e-10 kg per second, varying greatly possible due to assumptions about particle sizes and their distribution. This massive evaporation could be mitigated by physical forces and external pressure within the planet's escaping surface layer. Ultimately, this study highlights that planet mass and internal heat are not necessarily the sole determinants of mass loss in gaseous giant planets. Instead, dust particle sizes and mass loss rates are crucial factors in understanding planetary evaporation.

We establish a new proof of the topological Milnor fiber connectivity theorem using an approach based on the preservation of critical locus properties under deformation, which has far-reaching implications in the study of singularities and their deformations. This method is non-trivial and relies on non-compactness arguments, providing an alternative to other established methods. As a result, our approach offers a valuable tool that can be applied in the study of Milnor fillings and mixed boundaries in the context of singular spaces.

The emergence of big data has sparked the development of data analysis tools across various programming languages, with Daany being a noteworthy Python-based open-source application. This application processes data in CSV format and displays visualizations, including line and bar charts, to a web interface. Although Daany's success has been significant, issues have emerged when attempting to integrate data and styling customization within the same line of code, leading to complications within the existing codebase. As result, this study presents a comprehensive codebase overhaul to resolve these problems, incorporating modifications to Daany's core code in C#.net to address the identified issues.

In the scientific advancements of the past few centuries, mathematics has been pivotal in transforming abstract concepts into tangible realities. Prior to the 17th century, philosophers relied on qualitative reasoning to understand the world, but Descartes revolutionized this by emphasizing the power of mathematics in uncovering the underlying order of nature. By combining reason with mathematical analysis, scientists could derive intricate formulas that accurately predicted phenomena, such as trajectories. This new paradigm shift, however, raised the question of whether mathematical formulas represented the true universal laws of the universe, leading to a debate between qualitative reasoning and quantitative analysis in the Scientific Revolution.

The increasing importance of higher-order effects is becoming a prevalent theme across various fields of physics. In this work, higher-order terms in the Saha equation for ionization are explored, utilizing an innovative expansion based on the inverse of the ionization energy's magnitude. Utilizing an exact solution framework for coupled differential equations offers a clear and transparent approach to addressing the problem. We solve the equation for hydrogen and helium cases and presents the findings as supplementary data files to preserve data accuracy.

To analyze the merging of magnetic fields in magnetohydrodynamics, we numerically simulated two magnetic islands and supplemented the fluid model with an adaptively embedded particle-in-cell model to capture kinetic coalescence details. By injecting the particle model into regions of high relative velocity between the islands, we observed that the coalescing 'eat-back' process was accurately represented. Furthermore, we found that the presence of the particle model led to an earlier formation of the post-coalescence magnetic structure compared to a model based solely on fluid simulations, which showed good agreement with analytical results.

A programmer's skill acquisition process involves two crucial stages where they learn to translate an imperfect, natural language description of a task into an efficient and correct code solution. A recent code generation model, EnCoder, has been established as the baseline for this task. In this research, we introduce EnCoder's capability to learn both stages of code generation from abundant a priori code data and a smaller set of task descriptions. Notably, EnCoder's two-stage training method enables it to outperform previous single-train models and a multi-model approach that combines pre-trained NLP models and task-specific code fine-tuning, where these two methods were compared on five code datasets and EnCoder's two-stage training method showed consistent results as a significant improvement. As such, this two-stage training method brings about a major simplification to code training methodology by eliminating the need for external NLP models and large a priori code datasets. In addition, this research also delves into how the two stages of code training influence one another. In order to investigate this, we conducted two experiments involving how the two stages influence one another. In particular, these experiments examined whether the advantages of the two-stage training method can be sustained when the order of tasks is altered and whether these results are generalizable to other code datasets and tasks.
